title: Overview: The Purity Cycle
paras: About this overview. The following purity cycle, as it most commonly occurs, is presented as a succinct reference.
Note that almost every detail, however, can have deviations with potential repercussion, many of which are covered in this book.
Niddah state. The wife enters a niddah state (impurity) when menstruation begins.
Separation. Until she immerses, all physical contact with her husband ceases.

Ascertaining bleeding ceased. When at least five days have passed, prior to sunset the wife washes her entire body, particularly the private area, with warm water. Then, with a soft white cloth wrapped around the fingers, she internally examines herself. If this is clean from discoloration, again before sunset, she inserts a soft white cloth into her private area. This is removed after nightfall.

Seven White Days. If that is clean from discoloration, she begins the Seven White Days. During these days she wears white underpants, and sleeps on white bed sheets. Every day, she examines herself twice daily with a soft white cloth.

Preparation. On the last of the Seven White Days she scrupulously washes her entire body, including shampooing and combing the hair, brushing her teeth and making sure the body is free from intervening substances.
Immersion. After nightfall she immerses in the mikveh.
Permissible times. The times when marital relations are permissible.

Separation dates. On an ongoing basis, throughout married life, the dates when menstruation begins and finishes are recorded. From these are projected separation dates in anticipation of the upcoming menstruation.
notes: Other common causes include: premenstrual staining; childbirth; gynecological procedures penetration into the uterus.

title: From the Rebbe
paras: Innumerous letters from the Rebbe deal with Jewish family purity and marital life. The following presents only a small sample.
“...Often such a situation arises due to undesirable intimacy when forbidden according to the Torah. This is often caused by lack in knowledge of all the associated laws.

Therefore they, both the husband and wife, should clarify through an orthodox Rabbi knowledgable in these matters all the details incumbent in observing these laws. And from now on to keep these laws, keeping in mind that “there is nothing which stands in front of one’s will.”

Family Purity. “The channel to receive the Al-mighty’s blessing is behavior on a daily basis in accordance with His will. This is besides the fact that these are incumbent upon us as G-dly commandments. Each and every commandment is connected with a particular merit and force which it evokes.

It is known that the blessing for fertility lies in keeping the laws of family purity. Therefore, it is fitting for you to be exacting in your observance of these laws. Especially since during the course of time it is possible that some of these laws became forgotten and it is important to review them. With blessings that the Al-mighty fulfill all your wishes and waiting for good tidings.”
Strengthening Knowledge. “In these situations it is correct to follow the advice of a physician expert in this area, since we are to do whatever is possible according to nature…
However, and this is central, sometimes pregnancy is delayed resulting from lacking sufficient knowledge of the laws of purity.

Therefore, you should clarify through a rabbi who is very familiar with this area all necessary details. Even though being raised with a religious education you have sufficient knowledge, nevertheless it is worthwhile to clarify more, as it says, ‘there is no righteous person who may not have erred.’

LOVE & FEAR . “It is well known, and published, a particular letter from the Alter Rebbe. He wrote that the merit which is conducive to fertility is Torah study which evokes love and fear of the Almighty. Specifically, that is chasiduth. Therefore, you should make sure to organize and participate in a study group with some neighbors, at least three times a week. (In other words, three days should not pass without learning chasiduth.) Understandably, one of these three days would be Shabbos.”

Studying Chasidut. “I was pleased to receive your letter informing me about the study session you’ve established with your wife. May it be His will to bless you with success and soon with children; as the funnel to channel this specific blessing is studying chasidut.”

Spreading Chasidut. “… the more you increase spreading and strengthening yiddishkeit in your area -- on which the sages have said …. ‘One who teaches Torah to a child, is as though one had created him (Sanhedrin 19:b).’ Sometimes the reward is to literally bear children and fulfil ‘and you shall teach Torah to your child,’ in addition to the interpretation that child here refers to your student.”

Baby Boy. “Regarding your desire to conceive a son, I heard from my father in law something which he received by tradition, based on the verse… “bmeh yizkeh naar et orcho…” Psalms 119:9, that the merit to be blessed with a baby boy is through performing the mitzvah of hosting guests.

Of course, that is in addition to generally observing Torah and mitzvos. Though this may presently be satisfactory, there is always room to add since this is connected to the Al-mighty who is infinite.
Regarding Torah study, clearly you should make sure to set aside time to study chasidus….”
Baby Boy. In response to your request for a blessing to have a son...

It is worthwhile for you to make additional efforts to increase love for a fellow Jew, for the Torah and for G-d. It’s a known thing that the holy books write that giving ‘birth’ to this spiritual love is a catalyst for one’s wife to give birth to a physical son. From this it’s understood that strengthening our inner love through contemplating on G-d’s greatness (e.g. as the Rambam writes in the beginning of the second chapter of Yesodei haTorah) this will bring longevity and health to one’s own sons for many years to come. Therefore, you should decide, without the commitment of an oath, that until your wife gives birth to a son you will give a few coins to charity before the morning prayers. It is best if this charity is directed to helping feed students who have little financial means.

MEDICINE & TORAH . “The Torah directive is well known, that although the Almighty is the ruler and creator, nonetheless we are to make efforts in the physical realm as well. As the sages said, ‘the Torah empowered physicians to heal. Therefore, you and your husband should undergo another medical assessment through a physician who is expert in this field, and follow his advice.

Understandably, together with the above you should both add to Torah observance, particularly family purity, modesty, giving charity and praying to He who gave the Torah to fulfil this most worthy desire.”
“Through the mitzvah of niddah, purity and immersion, given to the Jewish woman, holiness and purity is brought into the family life.

Living in accordance with the laws of family purity a husband and wife merit happy, healthy children—healthy in body and soul, following the Torah’s ways, bringing true joy and pride to their parents.”
Education. “I was pleased to receive your letter of December 17th with the good news regarding your finishing the new modern mikveh building....

May it be His will that with the building’s completion and dedication will come a renewed effort in the true work, namely educating Jewish women toward fulfilling the laws of family purity, according to the letter of the law, in all homes, including those in your camp.

It is a known saying, ‘Purity brings... holiness... which brings chasidus... which brings ruach hakodesh.’ With blessings that you and all the house of Israel should merit: ‘I will sprinkle on you the waters of purity and you will thereby become pure... I will then give of My spirit to you, you will be My nation and I will be your G-d,’ with the coming of Moshiach quickly in our days.”

Life Saving. Regarding spreading observance of family purity, please keep this in mind. Imagine that the Almighty gave you the opportunity to save an entire city of Jews from destruction, G-d forbid. Surely you would jump at the chance to do so, and be grateful for the enormous merit which had befallen you.
Promoting observance of these laws is this, and much more. It is literally saving lives.

Women at the Forefront. It is the responsibility of all chasidic women to lead the way strengthening everything related to Torah and mitzvos in general, and specifically observance of family purity. They are the ones who should organise groups to shore up our adherence to a chasidic education and way of life, as it has always been in chasidic homes.

“...The Exodus from Egypt is the model for the coming redemption which is based on it. Regarding the Exodus it is stated, ‘In the merit of the righteous women in that generation the entire Jewish nation was redeemed.’ So too is the coming redemption dependent on the commandments of the Jewish women.
These three main commandments were given specifically to Jewish women—Shabbos and Yom Tov candle lighting, challah (kosher food), and family purity.

These are all connected to basic human needs, and are conceptually connected also to the G-dly service of non-Jews as far as their mission to “habitate” the world is concerned: Light, food and family life.

The Jewish woman’s job, however, is to accomplish these three mitzvahs in accordance with Jewish directives. Candle lighting is connected with Shabbos and Yom Tov, challah is connected to kosher food and family life to the laws of purity.
This is in preparation for that time when the physical world itself becomes purified and ‘All flesh will see that all is from His mouth.’”
notes: The subject of Shulchan Aruch, Even Ha’ezer.

title: Perfect Marriage
paras: Like all things so too is marriage comprised of two parts—body and soul.

The body is made up of the laws and guidelines structuring and directing its every detail. These include the laws of purity, which form the majority of this volume, as well as the laws of financial and moral responsibilities (see Appendix). The latter, are the basic commitments pledged under the canopy (chupah): delegation of financial responsibilities, interpersonal relations and child bearing responsibilities. They begin before marriage and reach until burial, thus creating the family atmosphere and framework. This is the body of married life.

The body requires a vitalizing force, a spirit to enliven it. This cannot be legislated. It develops along with and to a degree due to the body of marriage. This is the emotional bond created between husband and wife.

Love, as achieved through adherence to a Jewish life-style, can be likened to a good wine, maturing over the course of growing together and building a common life. It ripens and is cultivated by shared experiences, overcoming common obstacles and raising children. This is the idea behind, “A man will therefore leave his father and mother and be united with his wife. They will be as one flesh.”
True emotion develops over time. It is anchored by an attribute of the personality called da’as.

Da’as means personalized integrated knowledge—knowledge that is lived. So too, the basic emotions between husband and wife are based and nurtured through the common daily partnership of life’s burdens and toils.

Take to heart the following pages of this chapter. Here we delineate the words of our greatest leaders, illustrating the ideals towards which husband and wife should strive. Accordingly, each partner matures from a self-centered awareness to one in which concentration is directed on the family as a unit. The ultimate goal is the successful working of this family unit.
Husband and wife, according to this outlook, do not see one another in competition. Quite the contrary, they form a team. The foremost ingredient of this team is mutual respect and consideration.
A marriage based in the laws of our eternal Torah is destined to be infinitely enduring.The Rebbe, Likutei Sichos, vol. 1, p. 36
By definition, there is no perfect marriage. Perfection is without flaw. It even suggests effortlessness. Marriage is not this.

Marriage is a framework in which two distinctly different individuals, from separate backgrounds and families, each with his/her own personal needs, form a new entity—a couple. Now, what really matters is the mutual good—the success of the marriage.

To suggest that this can be achieved in an offhand manner would be misleading. Marriages undergo evolutionary changes. They are dynamic. They begin as the union between two lives. With the passing of time, these lives adapt, and with the achievement of mutual goals (raising children, paying bills, buying a home) merge into one.
This is an evolutionary process unattainable so long as each partner continues to be concerned mainly with his or her personal satisfaction. This is simply not a marriage.

The key to a harmonious and wholesome marriage lies in the couple’s realization that they must satisfy one another’s spiritual, emotional, and personal needs. This may be a conscious effort and it may require work. It needn’t happen overnight. In fact, in most cases, it is not a fast process, rather, an evolutionary one. A marriage may start out in one style and develop into an entirely different one. Age, working to build a common life, and time all join together as allies towards building this unity called a couple.
How husband and wife should view one another is stated succinctly and clearly in the words of our most profound codifiers.

“The Talmudic sages commanded: The husband is to honor and love his wife more than himself. For example, any monetary wealth he may have should be used firstly for her benefit. He must not use intimidation for coercion. He should speak softly and endearingly, not abruptly or impatiently.
Similarly, they commanded: The wife should honor her husband, even to the point of feeling awe towards him.
These are the true paths of Jewish couples—pure in their marriages. These ways ensure pleasant and wholesome families.”

It is important to emphasize that respect is a two-way street. The husband is not to use force in extracting that which he wishes from his wife. He is to remember to speak to her always in a soft tone, one fitting a daughter of the Jewish nation. The wife, likewise, is not to take advantage of this and is expected to reciprocate the respect and honor that the husband needs.

Consideration, endearing speech, respect. These very qualities are stated explicitly in the marriage contract, the kesuva. At the wedding, the husband accepts upon himself all of these responsibilities.

This behavior is incumbent upon the husband the moment he signs the kesuva and places the ring stating: “You are betrothed to me, with this ring, according to the Laws of Moses and the Jewish People.” The Laws of Moses refers to the Written Torah. The Jewish People refers to all that is included in the Oral Torah and later.

In fact, it is not only in the realm of ethics that these qualities find expression. Throughout Jewish law similar examples abound. For example: In return for the husband’s basic obligation to support his wife economically, the wife is responsible for the upkeep of the household. “The wife’s household work burden is compensation for the husband’s financial obligations.”

If the economic level of the couple (or in some cases the social norms) allows for it, the wife has some inherent legal rights to request the aid of a housemaid. She can request assistance with those household chores which would otherwise fall into the realm of her matrimonial duties.

However, there are a number of tasks which, regardless of their financial status, the wife is not permitted to delegate in any form to someone else. These she must personally perform. She is to spread the sheets on her husband’s bed. She is to draw water for his bath and pour his drink. These are tasks of endearment and therefore must be done personally by the wife.

In a similar vein, the husband must buy clothing and jewelry for his wife prior to holidays. This is based on biblical law, “And you shall rejoice on the holidays, you, your children and your whole household.” Based on this verse is his obligation, according to his means, to buy clothing, and jewelry— items which will cheer his wife before the holidays.
“In today’s world, people emphasize the idea that everyone lives for oneself, concerned only about his or her private needs, salary, things with personal benefit.
In this regard, the Torah emphasizes the importance of the family.

The family is one cohesive unit. Indeed, it comprises two separate individuals, created uniquely different, with different roles. However, this doesn’t imply that each one is to fulfill his role for his own benefit.
The opposite is true. They work together, complementing one another. Together they form the basis of the family.
From the family is built the entire Jewish nation, whose goal is to enlighten the world that there is One G-d who rules it and gives life to all.
Every family has its role in the scheme of the world. However, this role is only fulfilled when husband and wife work cooperatively.

In a confused world, where the importance of mutual respect and cooperation are minimized, and people justify taking advantage of others for their personal gaing, it is the Jewish family’s responsibility to be a living example of ‘Love your fellow man as yourself.’
This is accomplished, firstly, by living this verse themselves.”

We are not suggesting that the goal of a harmonious loving marriage overrides the fulfillment of any of the laws delineated in this book. The guidelines found in this book, based on biblical verse, Talmudic legislation and accepted custom, remain incumbent upon us. Our intent, rather, is to accent what the Torah sees as a perfect marriage in its overall context, in the hope that this understanding will accompany us through the remainder of this work.
notes: See the end of Chapter Three of Tanya.
Ma’aseh yodeah tochos mezonoteha, Even Haezer 69:4.

title: Niddah
paras: Although not directly related to the specific laws of family purity per se, there are a number of issues which the husband should be aware of in the larger context of married life.

The time of the wife’s menstruation is, in many cases, and to varying degrees, an uncomfortable one for her. Even prior to the onset of menstruation some women experience the physical or emotional discomfort called Premenstrual Syndrome.

As a result of the uterus expelling blood, many women experience menstrual cramping (Dysmenorrhea). This is a biological phenomenon over which she has little control. Both of these subjects are discussed in more detail in the Appendix.

Even when not menstruating she must remember to carry sanitary pads in case menstruation occurs unexpectedly. She must constantly change them when soiled and constantly keep herself clean to avoid embarrassing odors caused by menstrual blood.

The husband should be aware that prior to or during menstruation, his wife may exhibit quite pronounced emotional fluctuations. They may be based in hormonal changes or result from increased tension at this time.

If during these times her functionality is impaired, or even if she is incapacitated, he should lighten her burden by accepting additional household responsibilities. If she is undergoing difficulties she should communicate them to her husband and, if possible, before they occur (see Appendix - Premenstrual Syndrome). This will allow him to understand her situation and respond appropriately.

It is wisest for both to realize that these are biological phenomena, embedded in nature by the Al-mighty. There is no one “at fault.” What remains is to alleviate, comfort, and ease difficult situations as they arise and this demands heightened sensitivity on the husband’s part.
When a woman experiences a menstrual discharge, it being blood which emerges from her body, she enters a niddah state....Leviticus 15:19

A woman becomes a “menstruant,” niddah in Hebrew, when blood leaves the womb. This is based on the verse, “and she revealed the source of her blood.” The source refers to the womb, where the infant is formed and it is from here that menstrual (niddah) blood comes.

A woman becomes a niddah whenever blood leaves the womb regardless of the cause; i.e., whether related to the monthly menstruation, an internal gynecological examination which involved penetration of the uterus, giving birth or spotting.

Even a minuscule amount of blood coming from the uterus causes the niddah state, regardless of whether it is moist or dry—even if there was no sensation of menstrual bleeding or opening of the uterus accompanying the appearance of blood.

This state of niddah, as well as the spiritual excision of both for having relations at this time is applicable even before marriage, even if there wasn’t full penetration and there was no emission of semen.

The other prohibitions associated with niddah, including kissing, hugging, and affectionate contact, also apply to an unmarried woman, since an unmarried woman has never left her niddah state by immersing in a mikveh.
Additionally it is forbidden to be alone with them in closed quarters (unlike one’s wife when she is a niddah—see Chapter Four).

There is no minimum age for a woman to become niddah. Even a girl who has begun menstruating is in a constant niddah state until she immerses herself in a mikveh for the first time before her wedding.
When a woman experiences a menstrual discharge, it being blood which emerges from her body, she enters a niddah state....Leviticus 15:19

The subject of this verse is menstrual discharge. The words which emerges from her body are seemingly superfluous. The traditional rules of interpreting scriptural passages state that nothing is purposelessly repeated. Our sages, therefore, understood these words which emerges from her body to imply that the niddah state is scripturally defined as intrinsically connected to a physical sensation called hargasha. In other words, menstruation as described here is one in which the woman feels something when blood leaves the womb.

Feeling the womb open to expel blood or feeling blood flow from the womb into the vagina are considered hargasha. On the other hand, it is halachically questionable if feeling blood flow in the vaginal corridor qualifies as a hargasha.
Note that many poskim hold it is doubtful if women, nowadays, can accurately discern a hargasha as halachically defined.

When we refer to menstrual sensations we mean those listed above, specifically and not premenstrual syndromes (PMS). These may be a variety of disorders occurring prior to menstruation, including bloating, tiredness, migraines and emotional imbalances such as anger, depression, or anxiety spells (see Appendix - Premenstrual Syndrome). Note that we are not referring to disorders during the time of actual menstruation such as headache, stomach cramps, backache, etc., commonly associated with menstruation (see Appendix - Menstrual Cramps).

If the wife has a menstrual sensation she should check herself immediately (within approximately two minutes) by performing an internal examination using a soft white cloth, as will be explained in Chapter Five.
If the examination reveals a substance whose color is considered pure, we assume that this discharge was the cause of the sensation and she remains pure.
Pure colors include:
White
Yellow
Blue
Green Impure colors include:
Red, as well as any shade of red whether light, dark or deep
Pink
Any shade of black, which is assumed to have been red which oxidized and therefore changed color

Any shade of brown must be shown to an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws If an impure color is found on the cloth, she enters a state of niddah—even if the stain is minuscule (i.e. the size of a dot).

If the examination reveals only the body’s natural moisture or nothing at all, the woman enters a state of niddah. The assumption, here, is that the sensation resulted from an excretion of blood which was lost before the examination.

A woman who felt her womb open to excrete blood or something flowing from it into the vagina but didn’t check, is rendered niddah because it is assumed that hargasha is always accompanied by a discharge, presumably blood. A woman who is in doubt as to whether she has had a menstrual sensation should check herself within two minutes. However, if she didn’t check, she nevertheless maintains her former status because of the doubt as to whether she had a menstrual sensation or not.

From the beginning of the fourth month of pregnancy, during the twenty-four months following birth, or after menopause, a woman who had a menstrual sensation, checked and found nothing, maintains her former clean status. In all these cases, it is considered as if menstrual bleeding has ceased.
If she wiped the outer parts of her private place and found blood, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted.

As mentioned above, today it is uncommon for the sensations accompanying menstruation to fulfill the halachic requirements of hargasha and therefore an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws must be consulted in all cases of doubt.

Menstrual bleeding appearing as it normally does, (even when the sensation of blood flowing was unnoticed), as well as when discovered through an internal examination without noticeable physical sensations, render a woman niddah. From a halachic standpoint, it is considered that the physical sensation was slight and therefore went unnoticed.

If there is reason to believe that staining originated elsewhere besides the womb, for example: vagina, urinary canal, bladder, etc., or an injury, cut, bruise, infection, or medical irritations, hemorrhoids, etc., an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted to determine her status.

It is preferable for her not to check toilet paper after wiping with it. If she did, however, check it and found a questionable color on it, she is to save it and have it shown to an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws.

If the wife performs an internal examination using a previously examined clean cloth and discovers a stain of any size, she enters the niddah state, even if she felt no menstrual sensation. The day or night it is found is recorded for the purpose of reckoning the next anticipated menstruation.

If she has any reason to suspect that the stain on the examination cloth was caused through a bruise or cut in her vagina or in that area, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted. He may base his decision partly on medical evidence. Nonetheless it is a difficult subject which can only be decided through a competent authority.

If she notices blood after urinating an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted. Here too, there are many details which will influence his decision. Some details which should be clarified before asking his opinion are: whether the blood was found in the water or on the seat, if she sat over the middle of the toilet seat or on its edge, if this is a one time experience or it repeats itself, if she felt pain or burning during urination, and if she ate some red food, such as beets, prior to this. In any event, these are just a few of the numerous factors the Rabbi will consider.

The sages asserted, “There can be no opening of the uterus without blood flowing.” This applies when something is inserted into the uterus, e.g., a medical instrument and not only when something is expelled, such as during menstruation.

Some internal gynecological examinations involve examining the uterus using various types of medical instruments. When the uterus is penetrated with a medical instrument, the niddah state almost invariably results, even when no sign of blood is present. Therefore, in the event that a medical instrument was inserted into the cervix or into the womb, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws must be consulted. In light of the above, it is advisable to arrange such procedures at a time when the woman is already a niddah. If this is not possible, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted.

Insertion or removal of an intrauterine contraceptive device, I.U.D., renders the niddah state. An orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted regarding spotting. Note: Contraception is permitted only in cases of physical or psychological danger to the wife.

An examination using the fingers only does not render the niddah state and she is not required to examine herself following such an examination. Examining the vagina, even using an instrument, does not render the niddah state. If blood is found following this, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws must be consulted. A standard gynecological examination does not penetrate the womb or cervix.

During menstruation, it is customary for women to refrain from attending synagogue, looking at a sefer Torah or praying while standing in close proximity to friends. This custom is in the category of additional purity, not based on prohibition. Therefore, she is permitted to attend synagogue if abiding by this will cause her anguish e.g., during the holidays when everyone attends synagogue, when she is with her son or daughter, when visiting synagogue is related to her giving birth or she has another reason for attending. At home, however, even during menstruation, women may pray, make kiddush and say all the blessings.

title: Source of Niddah
paras: A woman becomes a “menstruant,” niddah in Hebrew, when blood leaves the womb. This is based on the verse above, “she had revealed the source of her blood.” The source refers to the womb, where the infant is formed and it is from here that menstrual (niddah) blood comes.

A woman enters this niddah state whenever blood leaves the womb regardless of the cause and whether for natural reasons e.g. menstruation, spotting, giving birth, emotional excitement, physical exertion or because of medication, or an internal gynecological examination which involved penetration into the uterus.

Even a minuscule amount of blood exiting the uterus causes the niddah state, regardless of whether it is moist or dry—even if there was no sensation of menstrual bleeding or opening of the uterus accompanying the appearance of blood.

This state of niddah, as well as the spiritual excision of both for having relations at this time is applicable even before marriage, even if there wasn’t full penetration and there was no emission of semen.

The other prohibitions associated with niddah, including kissing, hugging, and affectionate contact, also apply to an unmarried woman, since an unmarried woman has never left her niddah state by immersing in a mikveh.
Additionally it is forbidden to be alone with them in closed quarters (unlike one’s wife when she is a niddah—see Chapter Four).

There is no minimum age for a woman to become niddah. Even a girl who has begun menstruating is in a constant niddah state until she immerses herself in a mikveh for the first time before her wedding.

Menstrual bleeding appearing as it normally does, (even when the sensation of blood flowing was unnoticed), as well as when discovered through an internal examination without noticeable physical sensations, render a woman niddah. From a halachic standpoint, it is considered that the physical sensation was slight and therefore went unnoticed.

Questionably Originated Elsewhere. If there is reason to believe that staining originated somewhere other than the womb, for example: vagina, urinary canal, bladder or an injury, cut, bruise, infection, or medical irritations, hemorrhoids, etc., an orthodox Rabbi who is knowledgable in these matters should be consulted to determine her status.

Previously Checked Cloth. If the wife performs an internal examination using a cloth which was previously checked to be clean and discovers a stain of any size, she enters the niddah state, even if she felt no menstrual sensation.
Even if she had placed this cloth in a clean secure place but only afterwards performed an internal examination and found the stain, she enters the niddah state.
Blood found on an examination cloth which only partially entered the private area causes niddah, as well.
The day or night it is found is recorded for the purpose of reckoning the next anticipated menstruation.

Doubtful Source of Bleeding. If she has any reason to suspect that the coloration on the examination cloth was caused through a bruise or cut in her vagina or in that area, an orthodox Rabbi who is knowledgable in these matters should be consulted. He may base his decision partly on medical evidence. Nonetheless it is a difficult subject which can only be decided through a competent authority.
If she notices blood after urinating, an orthodox Rabbi who is knowledgable in these matters should be consulted.

Facts which might influence his decision include: whether the blood was found in the water or on the seat, if she sat over the middle of the toilet seat or on its edge, if this is a one time experience or it repeats itself, if she felt pain or burning during urination, and if she ate some red food, such as beets, prior to this.
Opening of the Uterus. The sages asserted, “There can be no opening of the uterus without blood flowing.”
This applies not only when something is expelled, such as during menstruation, but also when something is inserted into the uterus, e.g. a medical instrument.

Some internal gynecological examinations involve penetration into the uterus using various types of medical instruments. When the uterus is penetrated with a medical instrument, the niddah state almost invariably results, even when no sign of blood is present. Therefore, in the event that a medical instrument was inserted into the cervix or into the womb, an orthodox Rabbi knowledgable in these matters must be consulted.
In light of the above, it is advisable to arrange such procedures at a time when the woman is already a niddah. If this is not possible, an orthodox Rabbi should be consulted.
During menstruation, it is customary for women to refrain from attending synagogue, looking at a sefer Torah or praying while standing in close proximity to friends.

This custom is in the category of additional purity, not based on prohibition. Therefore, she is permitted to attend synagogue if abiding by this will cause her anguish e.g., during the holidays when everyone attends synagogue, when she is with her son or daughter, when visiting synagogue is related to her giving birth or she has another reason for attending.
At home, however, even during menstruation, women may pray, make kiddush and say all the blessings.
During menstruation it is customary for women to refrain from entering a cemetery.

title: Gynecological Considerations
paras: Disclaimer: Due to the interwoven and complex nature of gynecological situations and procedures, an orthodox rabbi who is knowledgeable in this area should always be consulted. This applies not only when something is expelled, such as during menstruation, but also when something is inserted into the uterus, e.g. a medical instrument.

title: Stains (Kesamim)
paras: Some couples rarely have a question of purity based on finding a stain, while for others this may be a common occurrence. Regardless of frequency, a number of issues are common and important for every couple to bear in mind. Don’t be overwhelmed by the details. To put them in perspective: a question rising from a stain is usually one found on the underwear, bed sheet, or toilet seat. A question of purity is raised only when its color is red, pink, black, brown, or a color similar to one of these.

There are many kinds of dirt and stains from extraneous sources, unrelated to the wife, and the rabbinic legislation pertains only to those stains that are found—specifically. Therefore, one shouldn’t actively search for them. In other words, questions regarding stains should be dealt with as they naturally arise, and shouldn’t be created by the woman constantly checking every inch of material. It is in this spirit that when the wife is permitted, she is advised to wear colored underwear in order to avoid unnecessary questions of stains. If she has a medical problem involving a high degree of staining, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws and familiar with the relevant medical aspects of the situation should be consulted.
If a stain is found, the couple should not be embarrassed.

The wife should not be embarrassed to share it with her husband. This is a natural occurrence which should be dealt with in a matter-of-fact tone; no one is at fault. In fact, in many cases a “pure” decision may be rendered by the Rabbi. Secondly, neither of them should be embarrassed to show the stain to the Rabbi (in the event of a question).

There is no preference in halacha as to who should approach the Rabbi. Each couple decides for itself. Many couples find it easier for the husband to do this. Regardless, there is no reason for timidity. If a question must be asked, it is a halachic one as in any number of fields— kashrus, holiday laws, or the like. The Rabbi will render an impersonal legal opinion, perhaps after a few questions, but there is no reason for fear or timidity. Even if this involves showing the underpants to him. This is his job, one he is trained to do, and remember, this is halacha— Hashem’s will.

If, in spite of the above, neither of the couple feels up to approaching the Rabbi, or if they live far away and cannot, there is an alternative method. An envelope marked with an identifying symbol or sign containing the examination cloth or garment in question can be sent to the Rabbi, followed by a discreet telephone call.
Chazal said, “we urge on those already working with alacrity.” Therefore, here is the place to insert a passing word to my colleagues.

As a Rabbi involved with the public, I feel that the following points are important for us to remember. It is specifically because we are constantly dealing with the public that we need to consciously bear the following in mind.

We must bear in mind that people who approach with a question often do so with trepidation. Awe of one’s Rabbi, mashpia or mentor is a healthy attribute befitting the holy people, a nation described as “compassionate, generous, and shy.” Therefore, it is critical to respond appropriately.

If the person has difficulty opening the conversation, “you open his lips” even an unrelated subject suffices, for example, asking about his personal or family members’ welfare. Always step out of the hearing distance of other people. If possible, it is preferable to enter another room. Dealing with the question while seated will give the questioner respect and peace of mind, allowing additional related questions to rise in his mind.

Inviting the person to call or approach in the future with additional queries is advisable. The most important impression to give is one of patience and concern. Most people are busy working and going about their daily lives. For them, approaching the Rabbi is, as mentioned, accompanied with a fair amount of trepidation, especially in respect to such a personal subject. Inherent in this is the responsibility to increase our awareness of the needs of our people and to respond appropriately.
The Talmudic sages ruled that she becomes a menstruant—niddah—also when she finds blood stains on her body or clothes in places which suggest it originated from her uterus.Shulchan Aruch 190:1

This chapter deals with the niddah state brought about by finding a stain(s) on the body, clothes, or elsewhere (as explained further). This niddah state is rabbinic in origin. In other words, it was the Talmudic sages who decreed that a stain whose location indicates a probability of its having come from the uterus renders the woman niddah. The location provides the circumstantial evidence that the stain came from the uterus. Generally speaking, this situation arises when a stain is found on the underwear opposite the vagina, on the toilet seat, or on bed sheets.

This situation contrasts with that discussed in the previous chapter, where we discussed the niddah state that was scriptural in origin. There the blood’s origin was directly linked to the uterus. For example, its appearance was discovered through an internal examination, with the sensation of flowing blood, or seen after the opening of the uterus.

Although the niddah state caused by finding a stain is rabbinic in origin, the laws of separation, as well as the steps leading to purification are identical to those required for the niddah state described in Chapter Two.

Since the halachos regarding stains originated in rabbinic legislation, when halachically feasible they are dismissed as having come from another source. This is only to be done according to the directives of an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws. Many circumstances come into consideration. For example, if a woman was working with dyes or walked in a slaughtering market, as will be explained. This is illustrated by the following:
“Once a woman came before Rabbi Akiva saying she saw a stain.
‘Perhaps you have a cut?’ he asked. ‘Yes,’ she replied, ‘but it healed.’
‘Perhaps it reopened?’ asked Rabbi Akiva. ‘Yes, perhaps it did.’ Rabbi Akiva pronounced her pure.

Seeing the surprised look on his students’ faces he explained: ‘The sages decreed that finding blood stains can render a woman niddah but this legislation itself was a stringency. Therefore specific decisions within the laws of staining aren’t to be decided in a vein of strictness, but rather in a spirit of leniency. This is so because on a scriptural level only actual menstruation renders a woman niddah, as it says, ‘When a woman experiences a menstrual discharge, it being blood which emerges from her body....’”
This story is brought by way of illustration. However, one may not decide for himself in these matters but must always consult with an orthodox Rabbi who is expert in these laws.
By definition, it is the location of a stain which suggests its having originated in the woman’s uterus. Blood discovered through an internal examination, however, is niddah par excellence.

A stain can sometimes be dismissed as coming from some external source, e.g., a cut on the husband’s body, child’s crayon, etc. This is not the case with blood discovered through an internal examination. Therefore, a woman who found a stain on her body, undergarments, sheets, etc. should not perform an internal examination so as not to exclude the possibility of a favorable halachic ruling.

The term stain (kesem) by definition implies that it was not accompanied by the sensation (hargasha) regularly associated with menstruation. What must be done upon feeling the flow of blood or other sensations related to menstruation was discussed in Chapter Two.
A clean internal examination performed following the discovery of a stain does not nullify the stain.
If there is some reason to believe that the stain came from some external source, for example a cut or child’s bleeding, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted.

If a stain on her garment was lost before being shown to a halachic authority, and there was a doubt if it was the minimum size, the wife remains pure. During the first three days of the seven white days she is impure. In both circumstances, however, it is preferable to consult with an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws.
The laws of staining apply to post-menopausal, pregnant, and nursing women as well.
There are a number of stringencies due to finding a stain during the first three days of the seven white day period; for details, see Chapter Six.

The impurity brought about by finding stains is rabbinic in origin. The Rabbis limited their ruling, however, by stipulating that the following three conditions must be met in order for such a stain to render a woman niddah:
Its surface area must be at least a circle 11⁄16 of an inch in diameter (17 mm.), the size of a U.S. dime.
It must be found on a white surface.
The object on which it is found can “receive spiritual impurity” (mekabel tumah). In this chapter, those things which are mekabel tumah are listed.

Even if all three conditions exist, a stain may still be dismissed due to other extraneous reasons, for example, a cut or the wife’s handling of dyes. In all these cases, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted.

Stains with a surface area less than the minimum size are dismissed as having come from a crushed insect, even in places where these insects are not common. Stains found on colored material don’t render the woman niddah, since it was deemed by the Talmudic sages that such
notes: Mehaber 190:1. There are, however, no leniencies, as explained further in the text.
As discussed in the previous chapter.

title: Absence Makes the Heart Grow Fonder (Harchakos)
paras: The idea of no physical contact for at least twelve days a month is perhaps the one aspect within the Jewish marriage cycle which has most captured the public’s attention. In fact, half of the month, except during pregnancy, or after menopause, we aren’t allowed physical contact. Other areas of our behavior are limited as well.

If you are a couple preparing for marriage, you may have mixed emotions regarding this subject. You are anxiously preparing for marriage. The most marked difference between prior to and following the wedding night is that afterwards physical contact is allowed. This itself entails a sense of excitement. Yet along with this comes the abrupt awareness that during married life this will be limited to only half of any given month except, of course, in the case of pregnancy. Experience has shown that people become accustomed to these days. What may have seemed a long time at the beginning of marriage adopts much smaller proportions later on.

During pregnancy menstrual bleeding ceases. During these months the rules governing separation are not in force (except in special cases involving spotting and the like). Therefore it is very important that following childbirth the couple review these laws.

Studying the laws of separation together is, for a number of reasons, recommended. These laws, in particular, are addressed to both the wife and the husband. Jointly reviewing them will ensure that their knowledge is on par. This can reduce misunderstanding and hurt feelings. Misunderstandings on details in law can be cleared up together, leaving less room for mistakes.

During this time, you should attempt to lighten your husband’s responsibility by dressing appropriately. This is not the time to dress up. Although you needn’t dress unattractively you should bear in mind the effect your attire has on your husband and act accordingly.
Perfume should be reduced or eliminated if possible.

For those conscious of fashion or their contemporaries’ opinions, this may be a personal trial. But conscious effort should be invested in helping your husband wait for the time when you will again be permitted to him.

You should be aware of your wife’s feelings during this time. It sometimes happens that the wife feels “at fault” for the present situation. You should try to negate that feeling or at least not nurture it. The forbidden times are designed by the Al-mighty as part of the marriage cycle.

The times when physical contact is forbidden should be seen as essentially a time of replenishing. Any experience, when available on a constant basis, becomes bland. The best summer vacation will, after time, drag on, the newest car becomes uninteresting and taken for granted, and marriage is no different. A famous Rabbi once wrote that the on-again off-again nature of the Jewish couple is, in fact, the cementing element ensuring a refreshing, wholesome atmosphere between the couple—“as a newlywed couple on a monthly basis.”

Not only is there a benefit following the forbidden time, but also during this time one can strive to relate on a higher plane. The absence of physical relations is a perfect opportunity for increased verbal communication. This is a time when many couples rediscover deeper levels of communication, working out family problems and the like.

The laws of separation are in force whether in the days of menstruation or in the seven white days and there is no difference whether she is a niddah due to having a period or finding a stain.Shulchan Aruch 195:14

The Talmudic Rabbis forbade being alone with members of the opposite sex with whom marital relations are forbidden and the punishment for willing transgression, i.e., intercourse, is excision; for example, one’s daughter-in-law or sister-in-law. This prohibition, called yichud, was designed to ensure modest and proper behavior.

Relations with one’s spouse during the time of niddah are forbidden and the scriptural punishment is excision. Yichud should, therefore, have fallen into their legislation. However, due to practical considerations and obvious limitations, the prohibition of yichud was not extended to one’s wife.

Since the Rabbis allowed this closeness between husband and wife as an exception to the above rule, they saw the necessity to limit contact in a wide spectrum of other areas. These areas are explained in this chapter.

For a husband and wife to be alone, yichud, while the wife is niddah, two conditions must have been met. First they must have had completed marital relations at least once and second, there must be a time when she will be permissible to him again. The reason is that since they have already had relations and the present niddah state is only temporary, the couple will tend to be more relaxed and will more easily refrain from forbidden relations. An example where the first condition is lacking: they married while the bride was a niddah. An example of the second condition lacking: the wife having a skin disease which precluded her going to the mikveh.
The laws of separation are identical regardless of whether the reason for the wife’s present state of niddah is biblical (e.g. menstruation) or rabbinic (e.g. finding a stain) in origin.

Likewise, the laws of separation are equally strict both in the five day time period (see Chapter Five) and in the seven white days (see Chapter Six). Furthermore, as long as the wife hasn’t immersed in a mikveh, all of the laws of separation must be followed, even if many years have gone by since her last menstrual cycle.
The wife follows the laws of separation from the moment she realizes her change of status; her husband starts from the moment she notifies him, either explicitly, or through her actions.
A couple, while in the company of other people, is not permitted to be lenient in the laws of separation for the sake of keeping the wife’s niddah state a secret.
Even if a couple is sure that leniency in these matters will not create any additional feelings of intimacy they are, nevertheless, forbidden to be lenient.
It is praiseworthy to be extra cautious in matters of separation. It is, however, not recommended to create new stringencies which are not already recorded in codes of Jewish law.
The husband may not act leniently in any of these laws in order to persuade his wife to immerse in the mikveh, for example if there is tension or disharmony between them.
The following actions are forbidden during this time of separation:
Touching, whether through direct body contact or through the clothing.
Insignificant contact, even touching with the little finger. If this is done in an affectionate way it is forbidden by the Torah.
There are also some opinions that non-affectionate contact is also forbidden from the Torah.

Holding an umbrella for each other while walking, lest they inadvertently come to touch, unless the situation demands it. However, when standing or sitting and where touching can easily be avoided, it is permitted, since the chances of their coming into contact are diminished.
Passing an object to each other, even a long object, (where the chance of inadvertently coming into contact is unlikely).
Passing an animate object which can carry itself, for example a child or baby.
To remove or place an object from a bag, while the spouse is holding it, for example a shopping bag or purse.
For either to caress, kiss, feed, dress or give a pacifier to a baby held by the other.
Blowing lint off each other’s clothing.
Fanning one another.

Sitting on a sofa, bench, car back seat or swing when they can feel one another’s body weight is forbidden. If there is a great need they may do so if someone is sitting between them. If the bench is hard and secured so that they don’t feel one another, they may sit on it simultaneously.
Lifting, carrying, pushing or pulling even a light object together, even when other people are assisting.
Pushing a baby carriage together.
Walking a child, each parent holding one of the child’s hands, if s/he is too young to walk unassisted. However if s/he can walk unassisted, they are permitted.
If the husband is blind they are permitted to hold opposite ends of a common object, such as a stick, in order for her to lead him in the street.
This is only when there is an immediate need and no one else is available. The following actions are permissible:
When the wife is in bed, he may place the baby directly on her bed without touching her blanket or clothing.
It is permissible to simultaneously hold or touch a non-moving object, such as the dinner table.
The prohibition of touching includes not touching one another’s clothing while it is being worn. This includes parts of the garments which extend from the body, such as a long dress.
They should also be careful that their clothes don’t touch. Similarly, the blankets, covering them (which halachically are likened to clothing) may not come into contact.
It is permissible however, for the husband to touch his wife’s clothing while she is not wearing it or her bed sheets, even if they are soiled with niddah blood.

They may not sleep or lie, even while fully clothed in the same bed even if it is very wide and each has his/her own pillows, blankets etc. Furthermore, it is forbidden to sleep or lie in separate touching beds.

The beds must be sufficiently distanced as to ensure that neither they nor their blankets come to inadvertently touch one another during the night. It is advisable to place a nighttable between the beds, if possible. The beds may not be connected by a common headboard.

She is not allowed to spread his bed sheets or blankets while he is watching, and vice versa. To change the pillow or blanket covers is permitted. The former is forbidden since it may arouse intimacy; the latter is deemed a more mundane act.
He may not sit on her bed even when she is not present. She may sit on his bed if he is not on it, but may not lie on it in his presence.
In his presence, she may not bring even cold water, for him to wash his hands, face, or feet. While not in his presence, or if he turns his head, this is allowed.

She is allowed to prepare water for the sake of a mitzvah, for example negel vaser in the morning, to wash for bread and mayim achronim after the meal. This refers to the husband preparing water for his wife as well.
The following activities are forbidden during this time:
Tossing an object one to the other
Tossing an object up for the other person to snatch out of the air

Since eating together can lead to intimacy, the Talmudic sages required some sort of reminder of the wife’s niddah state. This is to ensure that they don’t come to share each other’s food directly, which could lead to untimely and unwanted affectionate physical contact.
There are two types of reminders: placing an object not usually on the table between them while eating and using different placemats.
The laws governing eating apply even:
When eating a snack together or sitting together just to drink
When eating with other people
When other people who are present might notice thereby compromising their privacy in this matter
If she entered the niddah state during a meal, the couple must begin acting appropriately
When a reminder is required:
A reminder is required even when sitting so far from each other at the same table that one cannot reach into the other’s plate.

Although two people eating together, one eating milk and the other meat, must have a reminder on the table to guarantee they don’t share their respective foods, the husband and his niddah wife (one eating meat and the other milk) can suffice with only one reminder.
Even when the husband and wife wouldn’t presently eat from one another’s plates due to a quarrel.
Eating with a different hand than usual, however, does not allow eating together without a reminder.
Note: The wife changing her seat from the normal place when she is pure is not a sufficient reminder.
A reminder is not required:
When one is eating and the other is just sitting
When they are sitting at two separate tables
Objects as Reminders. Placing an object between their plates allows the couple to eat at the same table. The following conditions apply:
The object must be one which is usually not on the table. It may be used even if it is usually on the table if placing it between them is a change from its normal place.
The object placed between them must be of significant height. There is no consensus on this height, some opinions hold it to be around one handbreadth.
If this object is removed, it must be replaced before the meal is continued.
If they sat down to eat and an object was already on the table they can nevertheless designate it as a reminder.
Someone separating them by sitting between them is not a sufficient reminder.
Food from which they are not presently partaking may be used as a reminder. A whole loaf of bread which they are not using may be used as a reminder.
Note that on Shabbos, in order not to arouse attention, it is possible to use the lechem mishnah instead of removing it from the table.

Eating on separate placemats, or one of them using a placemat and the other not is a sufficient reminder, as long as this is not their custom during the time when the wife is not in the niddah state. Folding the edge of the tablecloth and placing one of their plates on the table or on that folded part is a sufficient reminder. So too is one placing his/her plate on a napkin.
Eating out of the same plate is forbidden even if other people are eating from it. This includes not eating from the same bag, even one after the other.
The prohibition of eating from the same plate applies even when eating at a meal which is served due to a mitzvah.

This prohibition of eating out of the same plate, bowl, or bag is only when the food is consumed directly after it is removed from the vessel. For example, nuts, potato chips, french fries, techina and other dips. However, it is permissible when placed on their separate plates before being consumed. Examples are a few nuts, a few potato chips, pieces of meat, potatoes, salads, soups. The fact that it is placed on their separate plates itself is considered a reminder.
Tasting food in a pot to see if it requires more salt or spices is not considered as eating from the same pot.

Cutting pieces off of a loaf of bread should be done as follows: they should each cut a piece off of the loaf and place it on their respective plates and then eat it from there. They should not cut off pieces and eat them directly.
The same should be done while eating a piece of watermelon—placing the cut pieces on the table in front of them.

Eating out of separate compartments in the same serving tray, for example those used on airlines, is forbidden. However, if the food is in different containers sitting in the same serving tray, it is permissible, as long as a reminder is placed between them.
It is permitted to use the same salt or sugar shaker.
It is permissible for both to dip their bread or challah in the same salt dish. However, it is forbidden to consecutively dip their food into the salt dish.

It is preferable not to take salt from the salt dish one after the other in order to sprinkle onto their food. Rather the husband and wife should place some on their respective plates and then dip their food into it.
It is permissible to use the same butter or jam on the table as long as the bread is placed on the table or plate before being eaten.
The husband is permitted to consume the wife’s leftover food or drink if at least one of the following conditions exists:
She has left the room. He is allowed to ask her to leave the room for this purpose.
He didn’t know she ate or drank from the food or drink. In such a case, she is not required to tell him.

The food or drink was transferred into another plate or cup. This helps even if it was then returned to the first plate or cup. It is permissible to move the food or drink to another cup or plate for this purpose.
Someone else ate or drank from it between the wife and the husband.
These ‘reminders’ break the intimacy inherent in a husband partaking of his wife’s food.
The above prohibitions only apply to food and drink, not other things like toothpaste, soap, shoe polish, and shampoo.
Pieces of food in the wife’s plate that she didn’t partake of may be eaten by the husband. For example, if she tasted one of two pieces of fish the husband may eat the second piece.
The husband is permitted to consume food or drink tasted by his wife to check for spice, taste, heat, or if cooked sufficiently.
The wife’s eating one type of food from her plate does not cause the remaining types to become prohibited to her husband.
If the wife cut a piece off a loaf of bread the husband is permitted to eat the remainder. However, he is forbidden to finish her slice of bread or individual roll.
The wife is permitted to finish the husband’s leftover food or drink.

When placing food or drink other than water in front of the husband, she must do so in a different way from the norm; this is called a shinui. This is done by placing it with the left hand on the table or placing it not directly in front of him.
Someone left handed uses their right hand.

The prohibition of not preparing a drink for the husband extends only to significant drinks, not to water. Therefore she can pour water for the husband to drink and place it in front of him and also vice versa.
When tea or coffee is lacking sugar or milk the cup may be placed in front of him or her.
Drinking out of the same cup using two different straws is likewise forbidden.
She may place a serving bowl meant for a number of people on the table directly in front of him without a shinui, even though he too is eating from it.

When making kiddush, he may not ask others to pass his goblet to her—rather, he places it on the table and she picks it up by herself. This applies for other significant drinks as well. This is permitted when others drink before her.
To pour into a cup placed on the table directly in front of him is forbidden.
The limitations regarding the wife serving food or drink to the husband apply to his serving her as well.
The following actions are forbidden:
For the husband to intentionally smell the perfume on his wife’s body or clothes.
For the husband to smell the wife’s personal perfume even while it is still in the bottle.

For the husband to make the blessing on the spices, on motzei Shabbos during havdala, while they are being held by his wife. If the smell reaches him without his having to come closer to them, it is permitted.
It is advisable from a halachic standpoint for the wife to refrain from using perfume during her impure status.
The following is permissible:
The husband is permitted to wash himself using the wife’s leftover soap or shampoo even though it is aromatic.

The husband is forbidden to hear his wife sing while she is in the niddah state, even if she is singing together with other people. Even hearing her singing voice on a microphone or tape is forbidden.
It is also forbidden to hear her voice singing praise to Hashem while davening.
The husband may hear her speaking voice as well as her voice while she is praying or learning Torah.
If the baby is crying and cannot be soothed unless the mother sings a lullaby, it is permissible. It is preferable for the mother to go to another room, if possible.
It is forbidden for the husband to use a flame held by his wife to light a cigarette or a candle or to warm himself.
However, he is permitted to say the blessing on the havdala candle she is holding.
They must eliminate conversation or behavior suggestive of intimacy.
Conversation dealing with daily affairs, such as running the household, is permitted. They may not study together from the same book, perchance they come to touch.

They are not permitted to travel together, even when accompanied by other people, if the purpose of the trip is the enjoyment of the excursion itself. Travelling somewhere for another purpose (for example to visit friends or relatives) is permitted.
If traveling on a bus, they may not sit in adjoining seats. This is to avoid contact between them or their clothing on unexpected sharp turns.

If travelling on a plane with adjoining seats, extreme caution must be exercised against contact between them or their clothing. It is preferable to arrange seating on two sides of the aisle, if possible.
They are not permitted to take outdoor hikes in the mountains or gardens or foot excursions together unless in the company of others. To take a walk together, however, is permitted.

It is preferable to refrain from giving the wife a present during her forbidden times. There is room for leniency, however, regarding gifts not of an intimate nature, when bad feelings could result. He is permitted to bring flowers home in honor of Shabbos.
Looking at places on the wife’s body which are normally covered is forbidden even when looking through thin garments, even in a mirror.
Those parts of the body which are normally covered are:
all the hair on her head.
from the neck to just below the elbow. From there to the wrists depends on local custom.
the body from the neck to the bottom of the feet and including the bottom of the feet.

During this time, the wife should be careful about walking in the home with her legs exposed, i.e. without socks, or sleeping with her bare legs exposed at night, and should exercise modesty while nursing the baby.
The husband should minimize his gazing at permissible places if this creates feelings of intimacy.
In order for the wife to maintain her personal beauty and dignity, the sages permitted her to use makeup sparingly during this time. However, she should minimize this as much as possible.

If the husband is ill she is allowed to help him recline and get up, to pass things directly to him, to tie and untie his shoe laces and to pour his drink for him. This is on condition that no one else is available to do so.
If possible, she should perform these with a change from the norm (shinui). Likewise, if possible, she should attempt to refrain from washing him and making his bed in his presence.
If she is sick, he is forbidden to touch her unless there is no one else available to do so and she needs it urgently.
