title: Intervening Substances (Chatzitzah)
paras: The previous chapter dealt with hafifah; the wife’s preparation for immersion. This chapter deals with intervening substances found on the body or hair after immersion.
A substance is considered to be intervening, from the Torah’s standpoint, when it covers the majority of the body and the woman is particular in not allowing such a substance to remain on her body.

The Talmudic Rabbis ruled that a substance on the body invalidates the immersion, even if it fulfills only one of these conditions. This stringency was designed to act as a fence guarding against immersion when both conditions are present.

Subsequently, it was ruled that all items should be removed before immersion, even if they are very small, loose fitting, and one is not particular about their presence. These, however, do not invalidate the immersion after the fact. Furthermore, when their removal is impossible, very painful, or particularly complicated, immersion is nonetheless permitted, in consultation with an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws.
It is of great importance that the woman wash and examine her body thoroughly before immersing in the mikveh to ensure that there are no intervening substances.
Note that no intervening substance (hatzitza) whatsoever should be allowed, and this is the purpose of the preparation for the immersion (see Chapter Seven).
Therefore, situations described on the following pages where we note that immersion is not invalidated, refer to those discovered after the fact, i.e. after immersion.
In the following pages we will delineate situations and substances which constitute a problem of hatzitza.
Knots. Two hairs which remained knotted, whether together or to two separate hairs do not invalidate the immersion.
One knotted hair, whether around itself or another hair invalidates the immersion, if she is usually particular in ensuring that not even one hair remains knotted.

However, if she is not normally so cautious, this one knotted hair does not invalidate her immersion. In other words, the law depends on her personal fastidiousness, even if most others aren’t particular about one knotted hair, if she is, it invalidates the immersion.

Perspiration causing most of the hair on her head or under her armpits to cling together invalidates the immersion. Less than half does not invalidate the immersion, unless she is particular about this. Perspiration causing even less than half of her pubic hair to cling together invalidates her immersion.

Lice. As explained in the previous chapter, a woman should do whatever possible to remove lice or lice eggs from her scalp and hair including combing with a fine comb designed for this purpose, rinsing with hot water and pulling them out with her fingernails.
If she was negligent and did not try to remove them, her immersion is invalid.
Hair Dyes. Hair dye which is absorbed into the hair shaft does not invalidate the immersion.

However, if the dye has already been ruined to the degree that it is undesirable or will become ruined and undesirable because of the hafifah, it constitutes an intervening substance and invalidates the immersion.
Ideally, she should either completely remove it or redye it. If the time of immersion has arrived and this is not possible or involves tremendous difficulty, she is permitted to immerse.

Cutting. The hair, when clean and unknotted, does not adversely affect immersion and therefore she should not accustom herself to cutting it in preparation for immersion, which may cause it to be viewed as an intervening substance for her.

If she did accustom herself, however, she should indeed attempt to cut it and is permitted even during chol hamoed, the day before the last Yom Tov in preparation for immersion on motzei Yom Tov, sefiros haomer and the week in which Tisha BeAv falls.
If, however, she cannot get her hair cut, she nonetheless immerses at the proper time.
Bandages as well as medicinal creams invalidate the immersion. If a bandage cannot be removed, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted.
If she rubbed her hands together to remove dough, mud, or clay, yet strands remained when she immersed, this invalidates the immersion.
If she immersed with flakes or peeling of skin, caused by extended sitting in the bathtub, her immersion is valid.
Cuts. Dry blood on a cut invalidates the immersion. Moist blood or pus in the cut does not invalidate the immersion. If, however, they extend outside the cut they invalidate the immersion.
Splinters. A splinter completely below the skin level, even if it can been seen, does not invalidate the immersion. If it extends outside of the skin it invalidates the immersion.

Stains. Dry paint, as well as other stains which have substance, invalidate the immersion. However, if she removed as much as possible and all that remains is a trace, this does not invalidate the immersion.

Mucous around the eye, whether moist or dry, invalidates the immersion. Mucous in the eye: if moist—does not invalidate the immersion; if dry—does. It is considered dry when it begins turning yellow or green. If the night has passed, she cannot return to immerse again, or they have had marital relations, the immersion is valid.
It is best not to use false eyelashes. If she uses them, however, she is permitted to immerse, provided they are complete.

Contact lenses are to be removed before immersion. If she immersed without removing them, and they are the type which are removed regularly, especially if she removes them before retiring nightly she should remove them and immerse again. If this reimmersion causes great difficulty and she normally does not remove these while showering, she need not immerse again. If she normally removes them while showering or sleeping, she must immerse again.
If they are the type which remain in place for long periods of time, even while washing, her immersion is valid.
If she did not remove an artificial eye she need not immerse again.

Trimming. Even if one fingernail remained uncut when she immersed in the mikveh she must cut it and immerse again, even if there was no dirt under it. If the nail was trimmed until the end of the finger, she needn’t immerse again, as long as it is clean.

If, however, she discovered it only after having marital relations, the night passed and for some reason she hadn’t completed marital relations, or she can’t immerse again (for example if the mikveh is closed) even if the evening hasn’t passed, the immersion is valid.
All of the above is on condition that the fingernail(s) was cleaned before the immersion.

Dirt Under the Fingernails. Dirt discovered below the part of the fingernail which extends beyond the finger invalidates the immersion, since most women are particular about this. However, if it is such a small amount that most women aren’t particular about it, then it does not invalidate the immersion.

On Friday night, or Yom Tov, if she didn’t cut a fingernail(s) during hafifah the day before, she should ask a non-Jewess to cut it with her fingernails, if possible. If this is not possible, she can ask her to do so with a scissors or clipper. Regarding a toenail, however, she need not have it trimmed, rather suffices by cleaning beneath it.

Dirt found under the part of the nail which does not extend beyond the finger does not invalidate the immersion, since most women are not so particular about this. However, if she is particular, then it constitutes an intervening substance for her and invalidates the immersion.
Dough or excrement found under any part of the fingernail, even that part which does not extend beyond the finger, invalidates the immersion.
Partially Torn Fingernails. A fingernail partially torn across its width, whether torn more than half (Diagram 1), or less than half (Diagram 2), invalidates the immersion.
In either case she should remove the part remaining and immerse again, unless they already had marital relations, the night has passed or it would be extremely difficult to immerse again.

A woman who insists on leaving her manicured nails long or her artificial nails on is, nonetheless, permitted to immerse, particularly if requiring their removal will cause her to avoid using the mikveh. Ideally, though, all nails are to be trimmed, as explained in Chapter Seven.
If she did not remove nail polish, which was complete, her immersion is nonetheless valid.
Toenails. If a woman forgot to cut her toenails before immersing in the mikveh, it is best to cut them and to immerse again as described above.
However, if she didn’t immerse again and if a lot of effort would be required to do this, one can allow her immersion, even if another immersion is possible.

In the event of an ingrown toenail, when the doctors prescribed lifting it by putting cotton under it to allow it to grow out properly, a woman should remove the cotton before immersion in the mikveh. Such a nail need not be cut.
Dirt found under the part of the toenail which does not extend beyond the toe does not invalidate the immersion, unless she is particular about this.

The verse “And he shall immerse his entire body in the water” indicates that only the external part of the body, the skin must come into contact with the mikveh’s waters, not the enclosed or hidden parts such as the mouth, nose and private place. Although not requiring actual contact, they must nevertheless be clean of intervening substances and fit to come into contact with the water.

One explanation traces this back to the seemingly superfluous word “entire” in the verse “and he shall immerse his entire body in the mikveh’s waters.” Another explanation traces it to rabbinic legislation seeking to diminish differentiation between the external (skin) and internal parts of the body, the reason being that one might think that just as the hidden parts of the body (like the teeth) needn’t be clean of intervening substances, so too the revealed parts of the body.
An I.U.D. does not negatively affect immersion in the mikveh.

Teeth. If in spite of the requirement to clean and check the teeth, as explained in Chapter Seven, a woman failed to do so, yet found them free from intervening substances after immersion, she need not repeat the immersion.

Finding some substance stuck to or wedged between the teeth, for example, a bone splinter, meat, or tomato peel, invalidates her immersion. Finding a small substance such as a piece of meat in the mouth, not attached or wedged between the teeth, does not invalidate the immersion.

Permanent tooth fillings, even in all her teeth, permanent crowns, and permanent artificial teeth do not invalidate the immersion. Regarding temporary fillings or crowns, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted.

She must take out removable artificial teeth. Failing to do so requires removal and immersion again. If the night has passed, they had marital relations or immersing again involves great difficulty, her immersion is valid.
Regarding other situations of teeth in need of undergoing dental treatment, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted.

Nose. Although it is best to clean the nose as much as possible, nonetheless dirt remaining concealed deep inside does not invalidate the immersion. Since most people are particular about it, dirt remaining near the entrance of the nose does invalidate the immersion.

Ears. Dirt found cleaving to the external part of the ear invalidates the immersion. Dirt found in the ear canal does not invalidate the immersion. However, if repeating the immersion after the dirt has been removed can be achieved with little effort, it is best to do so.
If, following immersion, she discovered she had not removed a loose earring or other loose jewelry such as a bracelet, ankle bracelet, or necklace, her immersion is valid.

If she wore a very tight ring during immersion and already had marital relations, the immersion is valid. This refers to a woman who is not careful to remove it while kneading dough or other activities.
notes: Even if it doesn’t cover the majority of the body in one place, but rather its combined surface areas does. See Mehaber 198:5. The hair is viewed as an independent body when considering if a substance covers its majority. Some say this refers to each hairy area. Some say this rule refers only to the hair on the head.
Even if other women are not particular, Beis Yosef 198, Tur, Taz and Shach 198:2. Or most women are particular, even if she is not, Mehaber 198:1.
Even after the fact, Bodei Hashulchan 198:5.
Ramo 188:1. This is considered a latter stringency, not of the Talmudic era, Sidrei Tahara 198:1.
Bodei Hashulchan 198:15. In consultation with an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws.
Mehaber and Ramo 198:5. Since there are two hairs, the knot cannot be too tight as to stop water from entering.
Mehaber 198:6, according to Sidrei Tahara this refers to a case where it is not the majority. Poskim.
Mehaber 198:6, Taz 198:10. “Less than half,” Tahara Kehalacha 20:15.
Shach 198:58. Shiurei Shevet HaLevy on Mehaber 198:47.

Mehaber 198:17, Shiurei Shevet HaLevy and Darchei Tahara. Two reasons: the dye doesn’t have a substance, rather only a color and she isn’t particular about its being there; to the contrary, she wants it there, Beis Yosef, Bodei Hashulchan 198:118. See Shach 198:21. Some poskim require its removal. Each woman should clarify her community’s custom.
On condition that it is completely immersed.
Shiurei Shevet HaLevy on Ramo 198:20. Ideally she should not have a haircut the three days prior to immersing, as explained in Chapter Seven.
Tahara Kehalacha 19:83 see note 233, Shiurei Shevet HaLevy on Mehaber 198:20.
Shiurei Shevet HaLevy on Mehaber 198:20. Igros Moshe Yoreh Deah (2) section 80. Bodei Hashulchan 198:148.
Shach 198:13. Darchei Teshuva 198:30. This leniency refers only to mucous in the eye.
Due to halachic discussion whether they are intervening substances.
Igros Moshe Yoreh Deah (2) section 62. I.e. they have not begun to peel off.
Igros Moshe Yoreh Deah (1) section 104. Gefen Porioh 5:8.
Ma’haram me’lublin brought in Shach 198:25, poskim.
“Having marital relations is sufficient to retroactively validate her immersion, so too is the fact that she isn’t able to immerse again,” Bodei Hashulchan Tziyonim 198:280.
And she is also not particular.
Torn more than half, Bodei Hashulchan 198:159, 198:146; and, when torn less than half, Bodei Hashulchan 198:156.
Both explained at length in Bodei Hashulchan 198:176, see sources in Tziyonim.
Only when permitted through consultation with an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws.
“Free-floating coins in the mouth do not, after the fact, invalidate the immersion, since the entrance of water is not inhibited,” Darchei Teshuva 198:74 in the name of the Tur.
Even if a bit juts out, but not enough that she goes to repair it, Shiurei Shevet HaLevy on 198:24.
Bodei Hashulchan 198:179. Shut Tzemach Tzedek section 160, poskim.

Some poskim place its permissibility in doubt, Bodei Hashulchan beginning of 198:179. Some poskim require its remaining for at least thirty days following immersion (Bodei Hashulchan 198:179) or from its placement, Shiurei Shevet HaLevy on Mehaber 198:24 according to Tahara Kehalacha 20:42. Others suffice with its remaining seven days, especially in extremely inconvenient circumstances, Shiurei Shevet HaLevy on Mehaber 198:24, see Tahara Kehalacha 20:42 note 149. Yet others mention no minimum time, Igros Moshe Yoreh Deah (1) section 97, Darchei Tahara Chapter 16. The halachic guidelines surrounding temporary crowns are the same as the above, Bodei Hashulchan 198:179, Tahara Kehalacha 20:44.
See Bodei Hashulchan on Mehaber 198:43 in Beorim.

title: What Is a Mikveh?
paras: As stated above, only immersion in a kosher mikveh under competent rabbinic supervision causes the wife to leave her niddah state. It is critical to know that bathtubs, swimming pools, or Jaccuzis of all types do not suffice. Even if she had waited five days, performed a hefsek tahara, counted seven white days as required, but bathed in one of these, she retains her niddah state exactly as before.

In Jewish law there is room for immersion in natural bodies of water such as the ocean. There are numerous stipulations, not in the scope of this book. In the case where it is absolutely impossible to go to a mikveh and she must immerse in a natural body of water, she must do so only under the exact directions of an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws. However, it must be emphasized that there are many stipulations to be clarified.

Following are important suggestions directed to those supervising the mikveh. They are meant to facilitate a more pleasurable and efficient experience for the women using the mikveh, as well as to lighten the job of those working there, making the whole experience as relaxed as possible.
The following should be kept in abundant supply.

• Acetone for nail polish removal. Purchasing quality acetone, although more costly, is preferable. It lightens the wife’s work in removing her nail polish, alleviates the ‘Mikveh-lady’s’ helping her, and thus speeds up the efficiency of the mikveh. The acetone should be kept closed, to retain its strength. Bleach to remove stains from skin.
• Hand cream for women after their immersion, especially in the winter.
• Appropriate and sufficient mirrors should be supplied. Preferably the ability to view her back also (through two mirrors) should be offered.

It is important to design proper water drainage from the bathrooms. This will lighten the job of whomever is responsible for cleaning. It is also important to ensure that the sinks have working plugs. This is especially important to women with contact lenses.

Wise delegation of duties should be exercised regarding cleaning the bathrooms between women and at the end of the night. In mikvehs with a lot of clientele, one should weigh the wisdom of expecting the ‘Mikveh-lady’ to be responsible for this.

Working fans should be in place during the summer, as well as proper air circulation. Proper lighting is also important. The baths should not be too narrow, to ease use by larger women. Hand rails should be available to allow women to enter and leave the bathtub easily.
A menstruant doesn’t leave her menstrual state until she immerses. Even if a number of years have passed, she remains forbidden until entering a proper mikveh.Shulchan Aruch 197:1

The mikveh is the single most important ingredient in the purification process. Yet only its most external component, the mikveh pool itself, is visible to the eye. The information in this chapter is presented for the reader’s information, although familiarity with it is unnecessary for immersion to be totally valid.

The word mikveh translates as a gathering of water. A mikveh, or a gathering of water, refers to naturally falling rain water which has gathered in one place. Our sages fixed a minimum amount to this body of water as being that which the full body of a person can immerse in at one time. (This is the size of the otzar, as explained further.) Once this amount of gathered water exists, any amount of drawn tap water can be added (or connected through pipes) to it and then this water too becomes “kosher” for immersion.

Since it would be unhygienic to leave this gathered water all year long and impractical to repeatedly change it on a weekly or monthly basis, the following is done. At the time of construction, two separate components are built into the mikveh. On the bottom or side (depending on which style mikveh is being built) is a saving pool—otzar, which is connected (through an aperture(s)) to the ritual bath—that part of the structure which is visible to our eye. This ritual bath is filled on a regular basis with clean tap water which, as stated above, thereby becomes “kosher.” It is in this part of the structure that the woman immerses.

In mikvehs where the otzar is beneath the pool, the tap water immediately becomes “kosher” when it comes into contact with the otzar water, this contact continues through two apertures in the floor. Each aperture is one tefach by one tefach.
The above diagram shows:

1) The ritual bath in which the tap water is filled; 2) The otzar—pool of rain water; 3) The connecting apertures. According to Chabad custom there are two connecting apertures, generally one under the steps and one in the middle of a separating piece.

There are a number of halachic advantages to this type of mikveh. One lies in the reduced intermingling of the otzar (rain water) and the ritual bath (tap) water. As stated, the otzar water validates the tap water. To do so there must remain a certain minimum amount of original naturally falling rain water. This design facilitates that, since the heated ritual bath water naturally remains above the cooler otzar water. This difference in temperature, since warm water rises, helps reduce intermingling of water.

Secondly, this custom requires two apertures through which contact between the two waters is made, unlike other mikvehs, which require one. This is to ensure that even if dirt built up in one of them, making it less than the minimum diameter, the second one remains intact.
An additional requirement of this type of mikveh is that the otzar is twice the size normally required in other mikvehs, further ensuring that the minimum amount of rain water is constantly present.
The above represents halachic advantages inherent in the design of this mikveh. Mikvehs of other designs, if under constant orthodox supervision are, of course, totally acceptable.

In mikvehs with the otzar on the side, a round hole, approximately three inches in diameter, is unplugged. This contact allows the “gathering of rain water” from the otzar to make the tap water kosher. The saving pool’s waters touch the mikveh’s waters and validates them for immersion. This hole should remain unplugged during immersion. If, however, it was not unplugged, the wife should immerse again while it is unplugged, if this is not difficult.
If necessary, unplugging this aperture is permissible on Shabbos.
1) The ritual bath in which the tap water is filled; 2) The otzar—pool of rain water; 3) The connecting aperture.
Orthodox rabbinic supervision is necessary:
To make sure there are no leaks, with the passing of time, in the ceramic walls or the rain water reservoir (otzar), something which could invalidate its kashrus.
To ensure that the apertures connecting the tap water in the bath with that in the otzar have a minimum opening.
That the rain water reached the reservoir properly and there remains a required minimum amount of it.
That it is clean from foreign objects.
That the depth and temperature of the water are as they should be.
That the building, especially its entrance, is situated so as to ensure maximum confidentiality for those using the mikveh.
Although it is not the focus of this book to go into these, the importance of competent and vigilant rabbinic supervision also applies to innumerable other aspects of the mikveh.
notes: Its distinction from a bath or pool is likewise not readily discernible.
As distinguished from drawn tap water called “mayim she’uvim”.
See Directions for Mikveh Construction, printed in the end of Shulchan Aruch Admur Hazoken parts 5-6. See a letter from the Rebbe printed in Sharei Halacha Veminhag page 108.
As distinguished from naturally fallen rain water.
Chabad custom is to build the otzar below; others build it alongside.
By virtue of its contact with the otzar pool of rain water.
Note that the “otzar cover” is removed when filling the otzar with rain water, see Directions for Mikveh Construction (paragraph four), printed in the end of Shulchan Aruch Admur Hazoken (parts 5-6).

Note that this is classified as otzar zriyah. “Regarding the mikveh: you wrote that they made an additional otzar on the side of the mikveh so that there should be a otzar zriyah. In truth according to the Rebbe Rashab’s mikveh, which is a ritual bath constructed above the otzar (according to the directions recorded by Rabbi Y. Landau) this is the best type of otzar zriyah, and it is superfluous to then have an otzar hashakah....” Part of a letter printed in Sharei Halacha Veminhag page 107.
Directions for Mikveh Construction, printed in the end of Shulchan Aruch Admur Hazoken parts 5-6.

This negates the Ravid’s contention “nason sah v’natol sah,” Shach 201:63. See Darchei Teshuva 201:128. See Directions for Mikveh Construction, printed in the end of Shulchan Aruch Admur Hazoken parts 5-6.

“I was amazed to read what I saw in relation to the directions to construct the mikveh above the otzar. These instructions are from the holy and glorified Rebbe Rashab (the father of the previous Rebbe, my father-in-law) may the memory of the holy tzaddik be blessed etc. may his soul rest in heaven and protect us, who sacrificed himself for the mitzvah of mikveh, as was known in the last generation. Also the greatest Torah giants of his generation discussed these subjects with him at length. “Anyone who is expert in the laws of mivkehs knows that there are many advantages to this construction style (the ritual bath above the otzar)....” Part of a letter from the Rebbe printed in Sharei Halacha Veminhag page 106.
See Directions for Mikveh Construction, printed in the end of Shulchan Aruch Admur Hazoken parts 5-6.

Another type of otzar sees tap water being opened directly into the otzar. From there, the otzar overflows into the bath. This is called otzar zriyah “growing/ascending.” These are less common requiring additional supervision ensuring a halachically required minimum rain water remains present. With time this could present a halachic obstacle and is a problem according to the Rambam Hilchos Mikvoas 4:7 and the Raved brought in Shach 201:63.

Shach 201:112. Note: “In answer to your question regarding discovering after immersion that the level of the water in the mikveh did not reach the connecting aperture: It is almost a surety that prior to this it was at that level and there was contact. It is hard to conceive that when those responsible filled up the mikveh they neglected to ensure sufficient height to allow contact. As is known, after contact was made, even briefly, according to many poskim there is then no halachic problem and the mikveh is kosher even in the first instance....” Part of a letter from the Rebbe printed in Sharei Halacha Veminhag page 105.

Mehaber 198:36. “It is the community Rabbi’s responsibility to keep watch, on an ongoing basis, that the “Mikveh-lady” is supervising the women’s immersion according to halacha, and not to rely on his having given her one-time directions,” Pischei Teshuva 198:21.

title: Immersion (Tevilah)
paras: The work of the ‘Mikveh-lady’ is one of the most important and sensitive positions in Judaism, for the following reasons:
The night of the mikveh is an intimate one, best kept the secret of the husband and wife. The only person privy to this knowledge is the ‘Mikveh-lady.’

Furthermore, the wife must immerse under the supervision of the ‘Mikveh-lady.’ Immersion, especially while being observed, is not a daily activity and many women are understandably uncomfortable about it.
Additionally, the fact that other women are present often adds to the wife’s concern that no one should see her. All of this adds to the responsibilities she has already, preparing for the immersion.
In light of the above, the role of the ‘Mikveh-lady’ assumes an added dimension. More than once we have heard of women preferring one mikveh over another because of the ‘Mikveh-lady.’
Although each woman is different, the following points are offered as food for thought.

The ‘Mikveh-lady’ should be sensitive to the woman she is assisting. A bride preparing for her wedding, for example, requires extra sensitivity. Often she approaches this night with apprehension. In many instances her mother escorts her this first night to the mikveh. In such cases the mother will wait in the waiting room or outside. Other women in the vicinity may know the mother and be able to deduce that this evening her daughter is immersing. This may, in certain cases add unnecessary distress to the daughter. Therefore, a little planning is in order. Perhaps the arrangements may be made ahead of time for the bride to come later at night when things have quieted. Or, a place for the mother to wait can be organized.

The ‘Mikveh-lady’ should be made aware any time a woman is being brought to the mikveh for the first time or is new to the experience. This will allow her the opportunity to act appropriately with added support and consideration.

Women have their emotional needs. Some women prefer the ‘Mikveh-lady’ to act casually; not to make a fuss of her; not to raise her voice, calling attention. Some women like the ‘Mikveh-lady’ to be supportive and friendly.
In general, the atmosphere created in the mikveh should be congenial and conducive to calm, undisturbed preparations.

In each mikveh different arrangements are in place. Some women dislike mikvehs where the waiting room is communal. They dislike having to wait in sight of other women.. Not all mikvehs have sufficient space to alleviate this. Each ‘Mikveh-lady’ and communal Rabbi should take note of this point.

When the women have finished preparing themselves, they shouldn’t be kept waiting unnecessarily. They should not be rushed to finish, on the one hand, yet when they have concluded hafifah, effort should be made not to keep them waiting unnecessarily to immerse.

The water in the mikveh should be kept at as comfortable a temperature as possible. The water shouldn’t be too hot nor too cold. The ‘Mikveh-lady’ should try to keep the material necessary for the hafifah in stock and in place. This means that there should be enough soap, nail cutters, towels, combs, etc. in the bathrooms, so that the women don’t have to request them.
Those responsible should make sure that there is sufficient light in the bathrooms for the women to properly perform their hafifah.

Another point which can cause unnecessary stress to women is when those in charge of the mikveh announce that the mikveh is closed at a certain hour and everyone should hurry. Of course, the ‘Mikveh-lady’ works long hours, but arrangements should be made in the community to allow for situations wherein a woman comes late to the mikveh and requires time after the scheduled hours. If this necessitates the ‘Mikveh-lady’ to receive financial compensation, this should be weighed positively by those responsible.

Remember, this is a special, intimate, and sensitive night for many women. Family life revolving around immersion in the mikveh is the single most important ingredient in the strength of every family and the entire Jewish nation. Every community must do its best to ensure the ultimate comfort and convenience for this night, even if this involves added financial outlay. No money could be better spent.

Experience shows that many women are tense about immersing in the mikveh. For some, this is based on fear of submerging. This may be accented by time pressure or fear of being observed. For others, this might be based on anxiety about performing the mitzvah properly.

Regardless of the reason, this is counterproductive. You should condition yourself mentally that no one is watching with a stopwatch and if submerging is distressing, you can go about it slowly. In fact, you should go into immersion happily. This night is the culmination of at least twelve days of separation from your husband and makes your intimate reunion possible. This is the single most important act in the Jewish family and should be done with joyous expectation.

In most communities there are fixed times when the mikveh is open and the ‘Mikveh-lady’ receives a fixed salary or stipend. In places where a “tip” is the norm this should be taken seriously, bearing in mind the important function the ‘Mikveh-lady’ fulfills, as well as the late hours involved.

Note: Only immersion in a kosher mikveh under constant supervision by an orthodox rabbinical board, an orthodox Rabbi or G-d fearing person specifically trained to supervise its upkeep, is able to remove the wife’s niddah state. Baths, swimming pools, Jacuzzis and the like have no validity whatsoever in this context.

If her husband is in the city, it is a mitzvah to go to the mikveh as soon as she is allowed, in order not to delay fulfilling the commandment “Be fruitful and multiply” for even one night.Shulchan Aruch 197:2

In the verses, “... and he shall not eat of any sacred offering until he has immersed in a mikveh. At sunset he becomes ritually clean,” purification is linked to sunset. Our sages connected the two (sunset and purification) by explaining that these verses indicate a condition of immersion. Just as there is a specific moment when the sun has “set,” so too must the immersion be completed at a specific moment. In other words, the entire body must be submerged simultaneously.

This concept explains the necessity for a complete hafifah, ensuring that there are no intervening substances, and the importance of being careful that the whole body, including the hair, is simultaneously submerged.
In fulfillment of, “Be fruitful and multiply,” if the husband is in the city, it is a mitzvah to go to the mikveh as soon as the situation is halachically permissible.
Even if they have already had children and even if she is presently nursing, pregnant or postmenopausal it is also correct to go as soon as possible.

It is critically important to be sure that the mikveh is under constant qualified rabbinic supervision. This is especially necessary regarding mikvehs found in outlying villages and towns, where constant daily use and rabbinic supervision are not the rule.

It is important to keep the matter of going to the mikveh private. She should go to the mikveh in a way that doesn’t draw attention. Keeping this night a private issue holds in relation to other women as well. However, it needn’t be kept a secret from a woman asked to supervise her immersion or to escort her to the mikveh.

If she is a guest at someone’s home where they are serving meat and her refraining from eating it may reveal that she is going to the mikveh that night, she should, nonetheless, not partake of the meat.
Even when other people may come to realize, for any reason, that this is her immersion night, she should not postpone it for the sake of secrecy.
Refraining from immersing as a way of angering the husband is forbidden.
The wife goes to the mikveh on the night following the last day of the seven white days. The immersion must be after nightfall.

Even when the community prayed the evening services early, immersion may not precede nightfall. This is regardless of the reason for her impurity—whether staining, hymenal bleeding following marriage, bleeding following birth, etc.

If she immersed before sunset on the seventh day, she should immerse again after nightfall, without saying a blessing. If immersion is very difficult or she immersed between sunset and nightfall she needn’t immerse again after nightfall.

Under extreme circumstances, when immersion during the night is not possible, it is permissible to postpone it until the eighth day. Examples: the weather is extremely frosty, the water is much too cold, or there is imminent personal danger such as crime, or she resides in a country where there are enforced night curfews, or if she is too ill. This refers to cases when these conditions apply on the eighth night as well, otherwise she must wait until then. However this postponement should be done only through consultation with an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws.

However, in such a case, the woman should perform the preparations for the mikveh during the daytime and not during the previous night, and try to keep the fact that she immersed during the day a secret from her husband until nightfall and have marital relations only after nightfall.
If the husband wants to travel during the twelve hours prior to the wife’s immersion, he must postpone such plans unless he’s travelling to fulfill a mitzvah or under extenuating circumstances.
When the husband is not in the city, the wife should not immerse in the mikveh. However, if there is a chance he will return, she should immerse.
She should not immerse in the mikveh if her next menstruation is expected to appear on this night for example this evening is her Interval Cycle or Average Cycle (see Chapter Fourteen).
If the husband is too ill to complete marital relations and the purpose of her immersion is in order to be able to assist him, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted.
On nittel nacht (the evening of December 24th) the wife immerses, however, it is best to delay relations until after midnight.
Mourning. During the seven days of mourning of either the wife or the husband, the wife does not immerse in the mikveh.
Friday Night. An orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted when her going to the mikveh on Friday night results from it being postponed from a previous night.
Tisha BeAv and Yom Kippur. There is no immersion the evening of Tisha BeAv or Yom Kippur. In such a case it is delayed to motzei Tisha BeAv or motzei Yom Kippur.
Depending on local custom, the woman walks from the bath to the mikveh covered with a cloak or sheet, with bath slippers on her feet.

It is necessary for a woman of at least twelve years of age to supervise and insure that the fingernails are cut and cleaned as required, that there are no intervening substances on the woman’s body or hair, that hair is unknotted and that the woman immerses her entire body, including her hair, simultaneously and completely .

If there is no woman available to ascertain that every hair has submerged, or for some reason it is too dark to discern this, the wife should loosely bind her hair to her head to ensure it completely submerses. She must be sure it is loose enough to allow contact between the water and her hair and that it doesn’t cause her hair to tangle or knot. The following are permissible for this purpose, in descending order of preference:
Loose fitting net of hair, preferably human hair although animal hair is also acceptable—with no elastic band which may prevent entrance of water
Loose fitting net of other material
Wool or linen cords or bands applied loosely

She may wet her hair and hand and ensure her hair submerged with her hand while loosely gripping it while submerged Failing to comply with one of the above stipulations invalidates the immersion and requires reimmersion.
Immediately prior to immersion, she checks her hair and body, both visually and with her hands to make sure there are no intervening materials on her body and no knots in her hair.

She should be careful that no dirt clings to her feet when she enters the mikveh, for example from the mikveh house floor. If there is, however, it is assumed to have been washed off by the mikveh water, but if the mikveh water was cool or cold it is best to immerse again if this is easily possible, unless she shook or wiped her feet while in the water. Regarding light dirt, it is assumed that the mikveh water washed it off.
She enters the mikveh until the water comes to about nine inches above her navel. A short woman may want to stand on the bottom step, which is designed and built especially wide for this purpose.
After entering the water, but before immersing, it is a good custom to splash some water on her eyes, under the armpits, and on the rest of her body, unless she is still wet from the shower or bath.
It is important that the water should be a comfortable temperature so that the women will be relaxed. If it is too hot or cold, the ‘Mikveh-lady’ should be asked, tactfully, to cool or warm it.
The woman should not spend a lot of time immersing in cold water, so as to preclude her hair from becoming tangled.

Ideally, immersion requires intention, kavanah, that she is doing so in order to leave her niddah state and not, for example, to cool off on a hot day. After the fact, however, she can rely on, for example, having immersed according to halacha or that she recited a blessing etc., as evidence of sufficient intention.
If her intentions in immersing were only to allow contact, not marital relations, because her husband is ill, nonetheless this intention suffices for marital relations as well.
A woman immerses her whole body once, paying special attention to lowering her head deep enough as to ensure her hair is totally submerged.

Her arms should be somewhat extended from her body as if she is walking (so that water can enter under the armpits). She bends forward slightly. The hands should be naturally open. The legs likewise naturally spread and naturally straight at the knees.

This posture is designed to ensure that the mikveh water can reach her body’s entire surface area (armpits, between the fingers, under the breasts, between fat folds, between her legs, behind the knees, under the chin). She need not lift her feet off the floor.
She then crosses her arms under her heart, (according to some customs, a hair covering is placed over her head) and she recites the blessing:
(Boruch Atoh Adonoi Eloheinu melech haolom, asher kedeshonu bemitzvosov vetzivonu al hatviloh.)
Blessed are You, L-rd, our G-d, King of the universe, Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning immersion.
During the blessing she does not gaze into the water.
The blessing is recited regardless of the reason for her immersion and niddah state, i.e., whether due to menstruation, staining, due to a strict rabbinical ruling, or hymenal bleeding.

She should not interrupt with speech between the blessing and the immersion. If the blessing was said mistakenly before taking off the robe, it should not be repeated. A bride does not say the blessing ‘shehechiyonu’ when immersing for the first time. A woman who returns to the mikveh as a result of finding a fingernail uncut, a new blessing is not said.

Then she immerses again. This second immersion is sufficient and she need not add more. According to local custom or family or community tradition additional immersions may be performed. However, a woman should be careful not to adopt a custom which could become a de facto vow, if she doesn’t intend to always keep it.
The second immersion is done as follows: her head is lowered so much that her body is close to a horizontal position in the water like a fish suspended in the water.
She should not hold or touch the walls. If she has difficulty, she can lightly touch the wall, however water should be able to come between the hand and the wall.

The immersion should be performed slowly and intentionally, not in a hurried manner. However if she did hurry, it nonetheless does not invalidate the immersion—so long as she completely immersed her entire body (and hair) as required.
If she is in doubt whether all parts of her body were in simultaneous contact with the water, due to her posture, she should immerse again.

It is customary for the ‘Mikveh-lady’ to declare the immersion valid by saying “kosher” or some other phrase with this same meaning. This causes the same declaration to be said in heaven and the meriting of holy, righteous children. If the ‘Mikveh-lady’ does not utter this pronouncement for whatever reason, the immersion is not invalidated.
The eyes should be naturally closed, not squinted. If she squinted her eyes, she should immerse again. If immersing again is not possible, her immersion is nonetheless valid.
The mouth should be naturally closed, not pursed. If she tightly pursed her lips, her immersion is invalid and she must immerse again.
Ideally, she should keep her mouth and teeth naturally closed. However, if she kept her teeth closed extra tightly, her immersion is still valid.

If she immersed while holding her hair in her lips, her immersion is invalid. These stringencies of pursing the lips, squinting the eyes, or holding the hair in her lips only apply when she is sure she did so in all of her immersions.
Not excessively squinting the eyes or pursing the lips apply to all women and should be emphasized to those particularly apprehensive of immersing, such as brides.
If she held a tight fist from before her hand entered the water until after she left the water, so that the mikveh water never came into contact with the closed part—her immersion is invalid.
If she made a fist after her hand entered the water, even if she held it until she finished immersing, her immersion is valid, after the fact.
One shouldn’t search for stringencies from which to invalidate the immersion; because there simply won’t be an end to it.

Rather, after performing the hafifah, combing, washing her whole body, exercising caution not to touch any substances which could intervene and immersing with extended arms and body, she shouldn’t allow various doubts to enter her thoughts. For example: whether she squinted her eyes or pursed her lips too much or similar thoughts.
For who is qualified to distinguish between something like squinting too tightly or not? (Ramban, end of Hilchos Niddah)
Meeting a Woman First. When leaving the water, the ‘Mikveh-lady’ approaches and touches her.

If she saw something impure first, for example a dog, cat, donkey, pig, or non-Jew, before seeing the ‘Mikveh- lady’ (or one of the other women in the mikveh even if she was niddah), ideally she should immerse again, if possible. This is done without reciting a blessing.
If, however, she already had relations or her husband is not in the city and marital relations will be another night, she need not immerse again.
If the ‘Mikveh-lady’ has any doubts whatsoever that the wife’s entire body, including all her hair (even one strand) was immersed, she must immerse again.
If there is no Jewish woman for her to see immediately following immersion, she can suffice by conjuring up thoughts of her husband or a tzaddik.

Washing. She should not rinse off the mikveh water, either in a shower or bath, before going home. If there is a definite need, e.g., the mikveh water was not clean or for health reasons, the wife is permitted to rinse off through a shower after returning home. In such a case the head and body should be rinsed separately and not simultaneously.

Verbal Declaration. Before any physical contact may be resumed, she must verbally tell her husband “I’ve immersed” or “I’m pure” or similar words. This is so, regardless of whether her niddah state was due to menstruation or staining.
His understanding through her actions alone is insufficient. Even her lying next to him does not suffice without her explicitly stating that she has immersed.

Mud at the bottom of the mikveh, although almost non-existent nowadays (most mikvehs being immaculate), represents a halachic obstacle. In such a case, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted.
In the event of no woman supervisor being available, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these areas should be consulted.
It is forbidden to stand on any vessel, chair, bench or other object, whether it receives spiritual impurity or not, while immersing.

After the fact, if she stood on an object which does not receive spiritual impurity, her immersion is valid, as long as this didn’t cause her to be unbalanced and therefore her body posture awkward, so that the mikveh water didn’t reach parts of her body.
Her immersion is invalid if she stood on an object which receives spiritual impurity, whether made of wood, bone, metal, skin, or otherwise.
In the event of anything, including mats, on the mikveh floor, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws must be consulted. There are many considerations involved in this matter.

If the wife requires the support of a friend or the supervisor for fear of immersion, physical illness or disability, etc., the following procedure should be followed: the woman supporting her places her own hand into the water and there she makes contact with the wife’s body. She should also be careful to keep only a light grasp on her .

If the mikveh’s waters don’t reach approximately nine inches above her navel, the wife is to lower her body in a more horizontal position as previously described, in order to facilitate complete immersion.

This is the case even if the low water level requires a completely horizontal position. In such a case, before immersing, she should splash mikveh water on all parts of her body, especially under the armpits, under the breasts, and between layers of fat.

If another mikveh with the proper water level is available, then it should be used. If she has a skin disease which disallows contact with water for medical reasons, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws must be contacted.

title: Intimate Relations
paras: It is imperative for the husband to be fully aware of his wife’s emotional needs. He must make special efforts to be supportive and considerate on the evening of her immersion. Each couple has its own way of relating. For some, sharing a cup of coffee and talking suffices. Others may prefer to learn a subject in Torah together. It is important for the husband to verbally express his affection for her to create an atmosphere of intimacy.

Generally speaking, there exists a difference between the male and female perception of physical relations. The word ‘generally’ should be emphasized, since each individual is unique. Interrelationships within couples vary and there may be cultural influences involved, as well.
Most women expect and need emotional support prior to, during, and following physical relations to a greater extent than men.

Each couple finds its own way of intercommunication. However, one should be especially considerate following the immersion. The husband should be compliant should his wife desire that he escort her from the mikveh. Of course, he should be careful that his presence does not cause discomfort to other women leaving the mikveh.

Endearment should be translated into terms appropriate to his wife’s personality. For some, expressing interest in their work is important. For others, sharing their difficulties regarding household problems is important. For yet others, interest in their health, compliments on cooking, or appearance are all areas in which the husband’s concerns evokes the wife’s love for him. He should, according to his knowledge of his wife’s personality, be extra attentive to these things on the night of the mikveh.
Remember, she has been waiting for this night too and, as a woman, has her emotional expectations and needs. Consideration of these needs are an integral part of the role of a Jewish husband.

In light of the above, the translation of onah (עונה) “time when relations are obligatory” adopts an expanded meaning. This night the husband’s role is not completed with marital relations, but more than this, he is to show extra consideration and affection, as well. He should realize that she also has her needs and he has an obligation to satisfy them to the greatest extent possible.

In this spirit, it is clear that to avoid seeming callous and self-centered, the husband should refrain from separating from his wife immediately following relations, but rather extend the feelings of intimacy.
Acting in a holy manner during intimate relations, the parents draw down refined trappings for the soul of their future offspring.Tanya, Chapter Two
This chapter deals with a very personal aspect of human interaction, hopefully to provide a clearer understanding and appreciation of this very important subject.
Judaism has a positive attitude towards marital relations, and views them in tune with our overall purpose as a holy nation.

It was not for nothing that King Solomon, the wisest of all men, chose the analogy of lovers to express the relationship of Hashem and the Jewish people in the “Song of Songs.” In Kabbalah and other Jewish literature, it is likewise used as an analogy of the dynamics of creative spiritual forces.

A couple who have marital relations during permitted times, with the appropriate intentions, merit to feel the Divine Presence between them. Rabbi Yakov Emden wrote: “When the husband and wife act fittingly during marital relations there is no act more sacred, wholesome, and pure.”

Judaism does not preach evading physical pleasure during relations with one’s wife. Rather, the Torah requires one to focus and direct oneself while engaged in marital relations, not to remove oneself from natural feelings, but rather to channel them in a positive and productive way. In fact, “when the marital act is not performed with love, affection, and desire, the Divine Presence is not drawn down,” as will be explained.

Interestingly, on Friday night, the culmination of and most significant time of the Jewish week, our sages encouraged marital relations. The reason for this is elusive at first glance. One might have thought that after an entire week of dealing with worldly affairs, Kabbolas Shabbos prayers in synagogue, kiddush, and the traditional Shabbos meal, we would be directed to study Torah, something conspicuously spiritual. Yet, we see that on this night, the sages encouraged man and wife to join in marital relations—not as a diversion from the spiritual nature of Shabbos, but rather infused with the same spirit.

In fact, the Al-mighty bestows His name on marital relations. When a man and woman combine in holiness and purity the Divine Presence dwells between them. The Divine Presence is called yud heh יה. The yud י is drawn from the man איש, whereas the heh ה from the woman אשה resulting in the drawing down of the Divine Presence יה during relations. The Divine Name is present in order to bring with it the soul (neshamoh) of the future child, as it says: “three partners are active in the formation of every child—the father, the mother, and the Holy One, blessed be He.“

Traditional Jewish sources assert that there is a direct influence of the thoughts and spiritual atmosphere between husband and wife on their seed and their offspring. Therefore, one should contemplate holy thoughts and envision righteous men during marital relations, since those thoughts will have an effect on the seed and create praiseworthy children.

The Talmud relates how Rabbi Yohanan, known as one of the most handsome (and righteous) men of his generation, used to sit outside the gates facing the mikveh. When asked to explain his behavior he replied, “in order that the women should see me upon leaving the mikveh and they should (likewise) have beautiful children.” As a result, when they engaged in relations with their husbands, they would afterwards bear offspring with similar traits.

Not only the future offspring’s physical appearance is affected, but even more importantly, the spiritual makeup. The Tanya clearly expresses this: “Acting in a holy manner during relations, the parents draw down refined trappings for the soul of their future offspring.”

The child formed from seed created through warmth will inherit the qualities of devotion and love and then manifest them in his/her personality. This warmth of soul results in alacrity of spirit and sharpness of mind in the child.

If his thoughts are filled with his wife’s well being, love for her, and thoughts of Torah wisdom, those thoughts will be enveloped and transferred into the father’s semen and have the power to affect the future child. Therefore, the quality of the future child’s personality is dependent upon the sincere love and devotion between man and wife during marital relations.
Conversely, if their thoughts are on mundane matters during relations, the seed which is created from those thoughts will form offspring in the same vein.
For these reasons, it is vital to know how to conduct relations in the appropriate manner.
In general, intentions are divided into four:
The most proper intention is simply for the purpose of fulfilling the biblical injunction to “Be fruitful and multiply.”

Another intention is to benefit the unborn child. Relations during the last six months of pregnancy are healthy for the infant: “causing it to become ‘fair’ and healthy.” Relations with this in mind are likened to the intention above, since here too the father’s goal is for the child’s benefit.

When the husband recognizes through his wife’s behavior her desire for his attention. (This has the same merit as the above.) So too when he is leaving on a trip, it is very likely that she desires his intimacy.
When the husband initiates relations for his own release in order not to spill seed. This also is considered a praiseworthy motivation, but it is the least of the four.

Friday night is a time specially set aside for (Talmidei Chochomim) to engage in marital relations. Semen is created from the most refined levels of the blood. The blood is drawn from all the various parts of the body and therefore a weakening effect occurs in the body when the semen is emitted.

However, at the end of the seven days of creation, when all of creation is renewed, man’s body is included in this process and is capable of transmitting semen, while not being weakened by it. It can be likened to a burning candle not lacking any oil, since oil is being added from another side. Another reason for the time is that it is a spiritual day not like any other and it is fitting that the souls of future children be drawn down on such an auspicious day.
Both undress while under the covers, their bodies remaining covered by a sheet at all times.
It is preferable for them both to be completely undressed however, the husband should keep his yarmulke on, and the wife should attempt to keep her hair covering on, if easily possible.

Before and during relations, it is important for the husband to appease his wife with hugging and kissing and in other ways. The husband is responsible to set the intimate tone, soothing and comforting his wife, speaking to her heart to arouse a yearning toward him. Unity cannot be without the intimate feelings of true devotion and sincere love for each other. Their future children will then inherit this warmth and develop into warm G-d fearing Jews.
It is customary for both the husband and wife to wash their hands three times alternatively. The husband then recites Mizmor LeDovid, and atifah bekitfah.
Translation

A psalm by David. The L-rd is my Shepherd, I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me besides still waters. He revives my soul. He directs me in paths of righteousness for the sake of His Name. Even if I walk in the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me. Your rod and Your staff—they will comfort me. You will prepare a table for me before my enemies. You have anointed my head with oil; my cup is full. Only goodness and kindness shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the L-rd for many long years.

“You who are wrapped in the bed sheets prepared [to take the wasted drops of semen]. Open your grasp! Open your grasp! Do not intrude on this union, and do not take out the drops. They are not yours or of your portion. Return! Return! The waves of the sea are calling you. I am cleaving to the side of holiness, encloaking myself in the sanctity of the Al-mighty.”

Food undergoes a number of levels of digestion. Only from the fourth does it become transformed into blood or semen. The seed created during the time when the food is being digested is less refined. Therefore, one should wait until the food is completely digested, allowing the finer parts of the food to become semen.

The most appropriate position is with the wife on her back with the husband lying on top. One explanation is that each should be facing the direction from which he/she was created. Man was created from the ground, “G-d formed man out of the dust of the ground;” and she, “G-d built the rib that He had taken from man into a woman.”
Their heads should be low and not raised high. He [or she] should draw her thighs upwards towards him.

He should remain engaged until he feels that no more drops of semen will be emitted. Therefore, he should not depart from her while he still has an erection. An additional reason is that it is best for the wife to culminate first Marital relations should be performed with sincere modesty and humility and the couple’s voices should not be heard.
The union between husband and wife parallels the union between the Creator and the Jewish people and has deep spiritual ramifications.

For this reason, the sages of the mystical tradition in particular, discouraged changing the position to the husband behind the wife. For the woman to be on top or their laying side by side during intercourse is deemed immodest. Several other behaviors are likewise discouraged as immodest: having intercourse on the ground, while standing or sitting. Kissing, or even looking at the wife’s private place is forbidden.

If the wife became niddah during intercourse, she must tell him immediately. In such a case: he ceases thrusting yet remains inserted. He ends bodily contact, elevating his body by raising himself on his arms and legs and presses his toes into the mattress. He should become full of fear because of the severe predicament in which he finds himself. He waits for his erection to disappear, separates, and behaves with her as a niddah.

Note that the moment she announces her impure state they are forbidden to enjoy bodily pleasure. Therefore, he is not to withdraw at that point, since doing so with an erection involves pleasure. Rather, he should behave as explained above. She too is to cease movement. Even if she only thinks she has become niddah, in other words she has a doubt whether she felt running blood or was only feeling him, he is nonetheless not to exit immediately. Even if he wants to exit immediately, so that she does not become pregnant, nonetheless, he is to do as described above. If he did not have an erection at the time she said, “I have become niddah,” he is to withdraw and separate immediately.
Regarding all of the above, to clarify a method of teshuva, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted.

The Torah requires a couple to approach marital relations in a loving and harmonious frame of mind. Halacha details a number of situations in which relations are forbidden because these conditions are lacking:
When there is hatred between them.
If the couple are in the midst of a quarrel, the husband should first appease his wife.

Against the wife’s will. Rather, one should appease his wife before relations take place. In this connection, our sages brought an example of proper behavior from a rooster. Before mating, the rooster stretches forth its full feather covered wing and swoops it down to the ground before its mate seemingly as if to say, “I’ll buy you a full body coat which reaches down to the ground.”
When either or both are drunk.
From the moment he decided to divorce her.
When he thinks about another woman.
When his wife is sleeping.
Relations during the day.
They shouldn’t speak of non-relevant matters or use foul language during relations.
After going to the toilet they should wait at least approximately nine minutes.

Even the subject of relations should be approached in a refined manner as we learn from our matriarch Leah who told Yakov in very refined terms, “come to me....” It is also modest and affectionate for the wife to beautify herself and act in a way which attracts his attention. The children who are created as a result of this will be just and proper Jewish children.

Marital relations are forbidden in a room with holy objects or books such as tefilin, Gemorahs, printed Chumashim, or prayer books, whether in script type lettering or the more commonly found modern Hebrew lettering. Relations are permitted if these objects are removed from the room.

Two Coverings. If removal is not a viable option, the above objects can be covered with two coverings. If one of these is a covering specific to that object, for example tefilin in their bag, the other may not be a covering specific for it, for example a cloth. Furthermore, even if there are many coverings which are specifically designed for that object, relations may not be resumed until another covering not specific for that purpose is added.
It is sufficient if the coverings extend over the top and sides, even if they don’t surround the object on the bottom.

The large plastic bag in which the tefilin and the talis are carried is deemed as specific for the tefilin (even though the tefilin are in their own separate carrying bag). Therefore, another covering must be added.

A hanging curtain, which completely covers the books, even if not attached on the bottom, in addition to one other covering suffices. A hard cover is considered part of a book not a “cover.” Therefore, two additional covers are required, except in extreme circumstances when no alternative exists.
On Shabbos, it is permissible to cover holy books or objects for this purpose. Note, that there must be two coverings to permit marital relations, as explained above.

Mezuzah. A mezuzah on the inside of a door likewise requires two coverings. Since the case surrounding the mezuzah parchment is specific for that purpose, another covering is required as well, for example a hung handkerchief.
A glass or plastic mezuzah covering, even if it is transparent, counts as one covering and a second covering is required, however, this second covering is not permitted to be transparent.
It is permissible to have in mind, while rolling the mezuzah parchment in paper or plastic, that this should act as one covering. In this case, the outside casing suffices as the second covering.

Sefer Torah. If there is a sefer Torah in the room, marital relations are forbidden, unless a divider is in place and the sefer Torah is covered. Removing it, however, to another room is preferable. Marital relations are permitted if it is in an aron kodesh box at least 17¾ inches by 17¾ inches by 58½ inches (48 c.m. by 48 c.m. by 144 c.m.). Some opinions don’t allow this unless the aron kodesh is attached to the wall.
Room Divider. A room divider allows marital relations while a sefer Torah, or other holy objects mentioned above are in the same room.

The divider must be at least 32 inches high(80 cm.), 76 inches long (192 cm.), and fastened well enough that it will not shake in a wind. This can be a sheet or other non-transparent material and serves to create a separate domain between the couple and the objects mentioned above. It is effective even if it doesn’t cover all the books.
On Shabbos it is forbidden to create such a domain.

Relations are forbidden when someone else is present and awake in the same room, even if a room divider mechitzah separates them. However, if their actions would go unnoticed, it is permitted. If the other people are sleeping, it is permissible when a room divider (mechitzah) separates them.
In the same room with a child too young to speak, relations are permissible.

While staying at someone’s home as a guest, relations are forbidden unless they have been given a separate private room where no chance of their actions being noticed exists and they take precautions to preclude soiling the host’s sheets.
It is forbidden to have relations outdoors, for example in a field, in an orchard, or in the garden, but rather, only in a place of dwelling.

Afterwards, they again both wash their hands as before. No blessing is recited. There is no prohibition of walking four amos before washing, as there is regarding the morning washing. Then some water is spilled on the floor, next to the bed (even a drop is sufficient).

The husband should continue to show affection and remain with his wife after relations. Some opinions prefer the husband to return to his bed a half an hour or so after marital relations, for fear that sleeping together may be conducive to nocturnal emissions, while others don’t. Based on self-knowledge, each person should act accordingly.

It is forbidden for the husband to mention Hashem’s name or to occupy himself in Torah until he washes or wipes with a wet cloth those parts of his body which came into contact with semen. As long as the semen is moist, wiping it off with even a dry towel suffices. On Shabbos, when wetting a cloth is forbidden, it is sufficient to wipe using a dry cloth or to pour water on those parts and then to dry himself.

Both husband and wife say Kriyas She’mah before retiring at night. Both wash their hands by pouring water on them: first right, then left. (Three times altogether on each hand.) Husband says Mizmor LeDovid (Psalm 23), then Atifa Bekitfah.
Both completely undress under the covers, staying covered all the time. The husband keeps his yarmulke on, the wife attempts to keep her hair covering on.
Lights are off during relations.
Afterwards, they both wash their hands (as above) again.
Some water is spilled on the floor near the bed.

title: Proper Times for Marital Relations
paras: Performing marital relations on Friday evening is considered praiseworthy by chazal and in unison with the spirit of Shabbos. In fact, they established this to be an obligatory time for talmidei chochomim and, by way of example, other Jews. This time is considered to be spiritually beneficial to the souls likely to be drawn down.
On Rosh Chodesh it is also considered praiseworthy to perform one’s marital duties.
On the night of the mikveh, one is obligated to perform his marital duties.

Marital relations during the daytime are discouraged strongly. Relations are only permitted under certain conditions, for example when the husband feels he is losing control of his yetzer harah—and then only when the room is totally darkened.
Yom Kippur. On Yom Kippur, the husband and wife are obligated to behave with one another exactly as they would during her actual niddah time.
These limitations extend to all areas of activity normally forbidden during niddah , there being no difference between the night and day of Yom Kippur.
These limitations begin briefly prior to bein hashmoshos on erev Yom Kippur.
They finish after the tosefos Yom Tov, even before havdala is made.

Prior to Yom Kippur it is permissible for the husband to swing the chicken used to perform kapparot around his niddah wife’s head. Likewise, the niddah wife is permitted to swing the chicken around the husband’s head.

Tisha BeAv. It is forbidden to touch one’s wife during the evening of Tisha BeAv, even though she is not niddah. It is also recommended to refrain from passing objects one to the other, as well as all the other limitations normally kept during niddah.
Most poskim hold that the above limitations do not exist during the daytime, however, it is preferable to refrain during the day, as well.

Likewise, sleeping in the same bed is forbidden, even if both husband and wife are clothed, they have separate sheets and blankets and the bed is so large that there is no chance of their inadvertently touching.
When Tisha BeAv falls on Shabbos, it is nevertheless customary to refrain from marital relations, in addition to the mandatory separation on motzei Shabbos and Sunday.
If the wife’s mikveh night falls on Tisha BeAv which falls on Shabbos, she should go to the mikveh and relations are permitted.
It is preferable to refrain from relations on the eve of the tenth of Av unless this is the night of the mikveh or he is leaving or returning from a trip.
As stated above, the most propitious time to perform marital relations is on Friday evening, whether for talmidei chochomim or other Jews.
The night of the mikveh, even when it falls on a weekday, has the same significance as Shabbos, in addition to being obligatory, as explained above.
Similarly, the evenings of Yom Tov and Rosh Chodesh have the same importance, as well as the evening of Sheviyi shel Pesach.
On nittel nacht (the evening of December 24th) it is best to delay relations until after chatzos.
The marital act is permissible during chol hamoed Succos.

According to the AriZal, it is preferable to be strict by refraining on the following nights: the first night of Pesach, the night of Shavuos and the night of Shemini Atzeret unless, of course, this is her mikveh night. For someone who has not yet fulfilled the mitzvah of having children, these stringencies do not apply. It is preferable to refrain from marital relations on the two nights of Rosh Hashonah, unless, of course, if it is the mikveh night.

Refraining on these days is a stringency beyond the letter of the law. Therefore, in the event of this causing undue difficulties or transgression of other laws, it is preferable to have relations even on Rosh Hashonah. In such a case, the husband should make sure to go to the mikveh the following morning.
