title: The Wedding Night
paras: Marriage is the single most important event in most people's lives: the choice of spouse, monetary expenditures, social and family ramifications on future offspring all depend on this night. The quality and substance of life rests on this night. Our deepest thoughts, justifiably, are invested in these subjects. Following this night our life is changed forever.

It follows that the choice of a Rabbi to officiate be approached with the same gravity. A differentiation between the levels of knowledge of Rabbis within the orthodox circle will not be drawn here. That point is mainly academic. It must, however, be pointed out that only an orthodox Rabbi should be entrusted to perform the wedding. Only he can be expected to have the knowledge, fear of G-d and compliance with halacha required to perform the ceremony within the letter of the law and with no unnecessary halachic complications.
“You are betrothed to me, with this ring, according to the Laws of Moses and the Jewish People.”Pronunciation under the chupah

Every bride and groom look toward their wedding night with a mixture of emotions: anxiety, excitement and nervousness. With the understanding that the couple’s mentors have prepared them for the physiological and intimate aspects of this night, this chapter will discuss the halachic perspective.
The week prior to the wedding the bride and groom should refrain from seeing one another, even during the daytime.

In preparation for the union with her new husband on the wedding night, the bride must go through the identical procedure to ascertain her purity at this time as she will during her married life, i.e. hefsek tahara, seven white days, hafifah and immersion. However, the timing of the immersion may sometimes be adjusted to the specific circumstances.

The necessity for a bride to undergo purification through a hefsek tahara, seven white days, hafifah and immersion apply even if she is post-menopausal. It applies in the case of a divorcee remarrying her husband, even if she is pregnant, and to a bride who is nursing.

When possible, the wedding should be planned for a time when the bride can expect to be pure. This enables every part of the wedding ceremony to be fulfilled in its intended form, including the consummation of the marriage, and prevents other halachic complications.

Nonetheless, one should not be afraid to proceed with the wedding if the bride will be in a state of niddah. In fact, the excitement of the wedding may cause a hormonal change and bring on menstruation unexpectedly, despite careful planning. (See further, Marriage While Niddah.)

The bride may perform the hefsek tahara (see Chapter Five) when she feels bleeding has stopped, without waiting the usual five days. The reason is that there is no chance of her having had relations directly before her period (see Appendix - Five Minimum Days).

If the hymen is intact, the internal examination by cloth will not reach as deeply in the vagina, but the cloth should nevertheless be inserted as much as possible. She should similarly insert a moch dochuk as described in Chapter Five. She should exercise caution, however, not to scrape herself and draw blood. In any event, wiping herself externally does not suffice.
If dryness makes checking difficult she is permitted to moisten the examination cloth with water. It should, however, be squeezed before insertion (as explained in Chapter Five).

The bathing and cleansing that is done before the immersion is identical to that of a married woman (Chapter Seven), except that the bride’s hafifah can begin during the evening, and need not begin during the daytime as other women.

Also, a married woman should preferably have short hair; a bride may keep her hair at its usual length for the wedding. This necessitates extra care in ensuring that no hairs are knotted and that all are totally immersed.

Every effort should be made so that the mikveh night is the night before the wedding. It is customary, however, to allow a gap of up to four days prior to the wedding to immerse. For example, if the wedding will take place on a Thursday night, the hefsek tahara may be on Sunday a week and a half before and the immersion may take place on the Sunday night prior to the wedding, but not any earlier.
During the days between her immersion and their marriage, she is to check twice daily, as she does during the seven white days.

So too, if she completed the seven white days, yet has not immersed, she should continue to check twice daily. After the fact, however, if she did not complete these checkings she has not invalidated her immersion as long as seven days have not passed without her checking at least once.

If the seventh white day falls out on the day of the wedding, they should arrange the chupah for a late enough hour to allow her to immerse in the evening before the chupah. If this is not possible, and the chupah will be in the evening, she may be permitted to immerse in the daytime, but only with the qualified advice of an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws.
The first time the husband and wife perform marital relations is called beilos mitzvah. It is preferable, from a halachic perspective, that this is fulfilled the night of the wedding.

The choson should try to complete beilos mitzvah with a complete entry on the wedding night. This excludes intercourse through incomplete entry to avoid causing the niddah state. It also rules out avoiding relations for the same reason.

In the event that intercourse is not completed that night, for whatever reason, for example fatigue or nervousness, either the choson or kallah should confide and take counsel with the person who prepared them for the marriage. There is no cause for shyness, and unnecessary confusion and stress can thereby often be avoided.

If the wife is a virgin, they did not complete the act, and she is still permissible, they may have intercourse for the first time on Shabbos, even though it involves hymenal bleeding. In such a case, they should make sure there was a proper yichud before Shabbos.

If the wife is not a virgin, they should not have intercourse for the first time on Shabbos or Yom Tov. In the event of its not being performed, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted as to their status with regards to yichud.

When the bride is a virgin, there is a likelihood that hymenal bleeding will be noticed. Unlike other instances when blood is found during intercourse, on this night the husband continues with the current act of intercourse until its completion. He remains inside until all semen has been ejected and then separates, even though his organ has not lost its erection.
When all semen has been ejected, he separates from his wife and they now behave as when she is in the niddah state. (As explained in Chapter Four.)

Even if no blood is discovered, she is nonetheless considered a niddah, provided his entire organ has entered. Furthermore, if he was sure that his entire organ entered during intercourse, even if seed didn’t ejaculate, she enters the niddah state, even if no hymenal bleeding is noticed.

On the other hand, if there is a doubt in their minds whether his entire organ has entered, she becomes a niddah only if blood is discovered. In other words, blood discovered causes them to observe the laws of separation even if it is questionable whether there was complete entry.

If there was not a complete entry and his organ slipped out, she is to check herself with a white cloth. If the cloth is completely clean, cohabitation is repeated that night if possible; if not, the following night if she is still permissible.
A lack of hymenal bleeding, even following full entry, is not uncommon.

After the couple notice hymenal bleeding, or there was complete entry, and behave according to the laws of separation (Chapter Four) nonetheless he is permitted to continue laying in her bed, off course, when she has left it. This is a leniency in relation to niddah times during the rest of their married life, when he is forbidden to do so.

Following hymenal bleeding, the newly married woman is only required to wait four days until attempting to perform the next hefsek tahara. This is a leniency in relation to the hefsek tahara during the rest of their married life, when she is obligated to wait a minimum of five days.

This leniency concerning hymenal bleeding is not limited to the first intercourse, but includes subsequent hymenal bleeding caused by intercourse, when only a four day waiting period applies before performing a hefsek tahara.
If relations occurred during ben hashmoshos, they are to wait a minimum of five days.

Of course, if the monthly menstruation appears during the four days, it will be halachically forbidden for her to attempt the hefsek tahara anyway. In this case, she is required to wait a minimum of five days before the hefsek tahara. Counting these five days begins from the beilos mitzvah, not from the appearance of menstruation.

As long as pain is experienced during intercourse, she is to check herself and the sheets afterwards for any signs of blood. Finding even a minuscule spot renders her niddah. When, however, intercourse has been fulfilled once with no pain, she need not continue checking as above.

At this point she is to check before and immediately after intercourse three times. It is best that both examinations are done as deeply and thoroughly as possible. If this is difficult, however, she can suffice with wiping before intercourse. However, the examination following intercourse must be done as deeply and thoroughly as possible.
The husband likewise checks himself three times following intercourse.

Most women have a certain number of days before which their menstruation does not appear—for example, twenty days following the last hefsek tahara. These examinations are to be performed before and after intercourse which occurred after these days. An orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted in assessing which days fall into this category.
When they have completed this procedure, and no blood has been found, she needn’t check anymore in relation to intercourse.

Experience shows that hymenal bleeding appearing even several times is not uncommon. This can often be rectified through a gynecological procedure. Since undergoing this treatment may halachically render the wife niddah, it is suggested to do it while she is already impure.
The choson should be told before the chupah if the bride is niddah.
If the bride is niddah on the wedding night, the choson places the ring on her finger while gently attempting to avoid direct contact.

In Chapter Four it was explained that it is forbidden for a man to be alone, yichud, with a woman with whom relations are forbidden and the punishment is excision. A man is permitted to be alone with his niddah wife if her niddah state is temporary and the couple has already completed relations at least once.

Therefore, if the wife was forbidden to the husband on the night of the wedding because she had not gone to the mikveh for whatever reason, or even if she was permissible on the wedding night but before they had intercourse she saw blood or a stain, they are forbidden to be alone together in the same room or apartment until she goes to the mikveh and is permissible.

The custom is to arrange for a boy between seven and nine years old to stay with the choson and, similarly, for a girl between seven and nine years old to stay with the bride. This is during the night. During the daytime, either one of these escorts suffices.
When the wife is niddah the night of the wedding, the laws of separation (Chapter Four) apply until she immerses and becomes permissible.
notes: In general, seeing one another prior to the wedding should be kept to a minimum or avoided. See Teshuvos Ubeorim Beshulchan Aruch page 436, “... even when the bride and groom are in the same city or two nearby cities, the spirit of Torah is that they should avoid meeting before the wedding....”
The bride and her instructor should ascertain the usual length of her cycle and project, to their best estimation, the best time of the month to plan the wedding.
According to the Rambam Hilchos Ishoos 10:6, the chupah is invalid if the bride is in a niddah state, but this is not the final consensus.

Some Rabbis advise the use of birth control pills to ensure a ritually pure status at the wedding. However simple and convenient this procedure may seem, its ramifications are much greater and can lead to problems including secondary fertility, G-d forbid, and long term complications of spotting and bleeding rendering the woman niddah each time. Aside from the possible medical dangers involved in using this drug. These factors must be weighed by an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws and familiar with the medical aspects. Shiurei Shevet HaLevy on Mehaber 192:4.
Tzemach Tzedek 196:28, Taz 196:7, Gefen Porioh 11:5. Note Degul Mervava and Pischei Teshuva 196:16 on Shach 196:20.
See Appendix - Five Days where it is explained the reason for the five days before performing the hefsek tahara. Here that reason is not applicable.
“A bride, kallah, needs to check herself just as a niddah,” Tzemach Tzedek 192:4.
The reason requiring beginning during the daytime (see Chapter Seven) does not apply, Nodah Beyehuda.
Short hair is much simpler to cover and easier to comb during hafifah. There is also very little chance of knotting this way.
A bride will often be accompanied to the mikveh by her mother or a mature friend in addition to the mikveh attendant to ensure that this does not happen.
For this reason she is not allowed to go to the mikveh on Friday night, since she is forbidden to have relations for the first time on this night, Ramo 197:2.
Tzemach Tzedek 193:1. In such a case it is assumed that there was hymenal bleeding, however it became unnoticeable due to its becoming mixed up with the seed, Mehaber 193:1.
Perhaps a small drop was unnoticed due to its minuscule size, Bodei Hashulchan 193:13.

title: Time of the Anticipated Menstruation (Vestos)
paras: This chapter deals with the prohibition of intimacy at the time when menstruation is likely to begin. Since intimacy during the time of menstruation (until immersion) is a very serious offense against explicit Torah law, the legislation in this chapter takes on greater immediacy.

To help you to properly observe the laws laid out in this chapter it is necessary to record, on an ongoing basis, the arrival and cessation dates of the menstrual cycle. Many poskim require this to be done in written form. Beyond this, experience has consistently shown that the only way to accurately observe this concept is to write it down. This is simple and not time-consuming.

Even if the couple is unclear about all the details of how to calculate these dates, it is still important to record the onset and cessation dates, as will be explained further. The reason is that their Rabbi, mentor, or confidant will have a much simpler job of helping them organize their personal records if these dates are presented in an orderly fashion.

Although many women have an intuitive awareness of when to expect their menstruation, it is not on this intuition that the couple is to base their actions, rather they must record and project these dates according to the directives of our sages, as will be explained in this chapter.
And you shall caution the Jews to guard against their impurity.Leviticus 15:31

Based on the above verse, the Talmudic sages, of blessed memory, established a requirement that the husband and wife separate on the date(s) when the next menstrual period can be expected to appear. This legislation was intended to prevent any opportunity for conjugal intimacy at the time of the anticipated appearance of menstruation.

The couple is to keep a record of the onset and cessation (as ascertained through a hefsek tahara) of menstrual bleeding on an ongoing monthly basis. Many poskim require this information to be recorded in written form and this remains the widespread custom.

Based on this information, the date of the next anticipated menstrual period should be projected and intimacy suspended on that date. This includes kissing, hugging, affectionate touching, and sleeping in the same bed. The other restrictions observed during actual menstruation (see Chapter Four) do not apply.
The sages determined that there are three commonly found menstrual cycle patterns: the Monthly Cycle, the Interval Cycle and the Average Cycle.

Even if a woman never falls into any pattern, nevertheless she should be careful to record these three possibilities since these are the most commonly found cycles and as long as she has no established fixed cycle, she must continue to observe these.

If she discovers any regular pattern, whether similar to these or otherwise, which appears three consecutive times, it may indicate an established fixed cycle. In this case, it is advisable to confide in an orthodox Rabbi or some other knowledgeable person to clarify the ramifications. (See Appendix - Fixed Cycles for further details on this subject.) The information in this chapter refers to a woman who has not established a fixed regular cycle.

As stated above, unless the wife has a fixed menstrual cycle, uncommon nowadays as defined by halacha, the couple must separate at the following times: The Monthly Cycle, the Interval Cycle and the Average Cycle.

The lunar cycle affects menstruation by influencing it to begin each time on the same date of the Hebrew (lunar) month. This is called The Monthly Cycle. In the following diagrams, the letter M refers to the Monthly Cycle.

This possibility represents the time interval from the end of one sighting of menstruation (hefsek tahara) until the beginning of the next. To calculate the Interval Cycle, the wife must have the dates of one full cycle recorded.
Another factor is that for most women, the menstrual period occurs on a regular thirty day cycle. This is called the Average Cycle.

In the Monthly and Interval Cycles, separation is observed either during the night half or day half of the date on which they occur. The night half is considered to be from sunset to sunrise. The day half is from sunrise to sunset.
In the Average Cycle, separation is required to last a full day. That is, from one sunset to the next the following day, regardless which part of the night or day the previous menstruation began.
Note: Only the Hebrew dates have validity in recording the time of the anticipated menstruation.

Additionally, on these dates, the sages required the wife to perform an internal examination to see if menstruation did in fact appear on the projected date. This is accomplished by wrapping an examination cloth (or any soft white cloth) around her fingers, inserting it as deeply as possible, and turning it around while checking all clefts and folds. She then removes it and visually inspects it for any sign of blood. If discomfort is experienced, the cloth may be lightly moistened with water. It is recommended to use the commercially distributed and widely available cloths which have reliable rabbinic supervision.

The examination is performed from the recorded time of day when the last menstruation began onwards. For example, if the last menstruation began at 10:00 a.m. this examination should be performed anytime from 10:00 a.m. until the end of the day. Or, for example, if the last menstruation began at 10:00 p.m. this examination should be performed anytime from 10:00 p.m until sunrise.

If there is no blood, the couple is permitted to renew marital relations, providing that the day or night span (or complete night and day span in the Average Cycle) have passed completely. Regarding the Average Cycle, the wife must explicitly state to the husband that she checked herself.
If there is blood, the wife enters the state of niddah. There is no minimum amount. Even a spot no larger than a needle point renders her niddah.

If the wife misses the examination and no blood was noticed until the end of the Monthly or Interval Cycle, relations are permitted, provided that the half day span has completely passed. Note that this refers to a non-established cycle. Regarding the Average Cycle or a fixed cycle, however, relations are forbidden until she does actually perform an examination even if she checked after much time has elapsed. If she bathed following an Average Cycle or a Fixed Cycle before checking, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted.
Remember, for all purposes mentioned, nighttime is from sunset till sunrise. Daytime is from sunrise till sunset.

Note: In this chapter and in Appendix - Fixed Cycles, we refer only to time or date related cycles. Noting a direct connection between bodily phenomenon such as repeated hiccups, sneezing or excessive yawning and the onset of menstruation may indicate a causative relationship. In this case, it should be discussed with someone expert in this field.
Although stains found on the body or on clothes may render a woman niddah, nevertheless, they are not considered factors when projecting the dates of the next menstrual cycle.
Even discovering a stain three consecutive times on the same date does not establish a fixed cycle. Even discovering menstruation twice and a stain the third time does not establish a fixed cycle.

The night or day blood was discovered through an internal examination is recorded for the purpose of projecting the anticipated menstruation. Furthermore, if this repeats itself three consecutive times it is considered according to the laws of fixed cycles.
The examination cloth must have been previously checked and found to be free from dirt or stains.
If she wipes her private place externally and finds an impure color, she does not record it to project the next anticipated menstruation.

If the wife becomes niddah due to a gynecological examination, giving birth, a miscarriage, or due to external influences such as strenuous exercise, this is not recorded for the purpose of projecting the anticipated menstruation.

Menstrual bleeding even from the fourth month of pregnancy or during the twenty-four months following birth is recorded for the purpose of projecting the anticipated menstruation. During these times she observes the Average Cycle, but does not establish a fixed cycle.
As indicated by its name, the Monthly Cycle represents the relationship between the beginning of menstruation and a certain date. (In these examples, M refers to Monthly Cycle.)
If a woman sees once or even twice on the same date, then on a later date, then the couple only need to separate on the second date the next month. For example:
Menstruation began in two consecutive months on the fifth. In the third month it began on the sixth. In this case, the fifth is disregarded and in the following month they separate on the sixth.
Even if she didn’t perform an internal examination on the fifth, nonetheless, since she didn’t notice menstrual bleeding, they need only separate on the sixth the next month.
The following is similar to the above example.
In this example menstruation began twice on the sixth. Then, unlike the previous example, the third month it began on the previous day (the fifth).
Nonetheless, the following month they separate on the fifth.
Some opinions hold that since the sixth wasn’t passed in purity the following month they separate on the fifth and on the sixth.
Since this question involves a difference of opinion amongst contemporary poskim, you should clarify what your custom is with your Rabbi.

In the next example, a date was recorded as the anticipated Monthly Cycle. Another menstruation began and she immersed in the mikveh before that date arrived. Nonetheless, when that previously recorded Monthly Cycle arrives they must separate. See the diagram:

In this example menstruation began during the night of the second. As a result, the Monthly Cycle for next month was set for the night of the second. Before this date arrived, menstruation began during the day of the nineteenth. In this case, when the second arrives it must still be observed the next month. Additionally, the new date (the nineteenth, during the day) must be recorded and observed, leading to two Monthly Cycle dates. Note that recalculations regarding the Interval Cycle are also necessary with the input of this new information.
If she began menstruating on the thirtieth of the month and next month has only twenty-nine days, she needn’t observe the Monthly Cycle the following month.
In recording the Monthly Cycle the dates remain the same, regardless of whether either month has twenty-nine or thirty days.

As its name indicates, the Interval Cycle represents the amount of time between the end of the last menstruation (ascertained through the hefsek tahara) until the beginning of the next. This time period is measured in half-day (day or night) increments called onahs.

Long cycles erase shorter non-established previous cycles. For example: in our previous illustration of the Interval Cycle, we recorded a cycle of 46 half day periods. If the next cycle were 47 half day periods or longer, it would erase and displace the need to consider the old cycle of 46.

On the other hand, shorter cycles do not erase longer non-established previous cycles. In the previous example, if the next cycle was 45 half day periods [or shorter], then the following month they would separate both on the 45th and on the 46th half day. However, now the woman begins recounting from the hefsek tahara of this last menstruation. The reason is that, as its name indicates, the Interval Cycle represents the time from the end of the last menstruation to the onset of the next anticipated one. Therefore, interrupting one counting necessitates a new count.
The Average Cycle represents the time cycle most women pass through from the beginning of the last menstruation to the beginning of the next menstruation.
Therefore, if a date was recorded as the thirtieth day from the last onset, but menstruation appeared before that date, a new count is made from this new sighting.

For example: The last sighting was on the 27th. Therefore, the 27th was recorded for the following month as the thirtieth day (Average Cycle). In the meantime menstruation appeared on the 15th. Therefore, a new counting is begun starting from the 15th. The thirtieth day from the 15th is the new Average Cycle, which completely replaces the old one.

Discovering a stain does not require a new counting. For example, the 15th of Nissan was recorded as the Average Cycle; finding a stain on the 28th of Adar does not necessitate a new counting or cancelling observance of the 15th of Nissan.

Even if a woman does not usually see menstruation on the thirtieth day; or does not usually see until after the thirtieth day, as long as she has not established a fixed cycle, she must observe the Average Cycle since this is the most commonly found cycle.
Regarding a woman with an established fixed cycle see Appendix - Fixed Cycles.

A doubt whether the time she discovered menstruation was before or after sunrise requires separation the following month during both night and daytimes. So too, if a woman has a doubt whether the time she discovered menstruation was before or after sunset, they must separate the following month during the daytime and the nighttime.

For example: Around sunrise time she discovered menstruation had begun but it is unclear whether this time was before sunrise (which is considered nighttime) or after sunrise (which is considered daytime). In such a case, the following month they must separate during the corresponding nighttime as well as the daytime.

The dates of the anticipated menstruation are determined according to the time when the last menstruation began. If it began during the night, separation will be observed during the night. If it began during the day, separation will be observed during the day. This refers to a normal menstruation which lasts a few days. Exception: If the menstruation began during the nighttime (i.e. before sunrise) and extended only a few hours into the daytime, then the following month they separate during the nighttime and that amount of time into the following day. When that amount of time has passed, she checks and if this internal examination is clean, she is permitted.

For example: The last menstruation began during the night and extended until 10:00 a.m. On the anticipated date, separation is observed during the night into the following day. At 10:00 a.m. she checks and if this examination is clean, she is permitted.

So too, if menstruation began during the daytime (before sunset) and lasted a few hours into the night, the following month they separate during the daytime and the following night for the same amount of time during which the previous month’s menstruation continued. When that amount of time has passed, she checks. If this internal examination is clean, she is permitted.

The reason for this is that, as described above, separation on the date of the anticipated menstruation corresponds to the last menstrual beginning. This menstruation lasted only a few hours into the following day (or night). This whole time is therefore considered its beginning.

title: Birth
paras: When contractions have begun, even if the womb has begun to open, she remains pure. Even when the hospital staff says the womb has opened two or three fingers wide, she remains pure, as long as she can walk without assistance.
When contractions strengthen to the point where she feels she needs to lay down to give birth or it is so difficult for her to walk that she requires assistance, she enters the niddah state.

If contractions reached this stage and then receded, indicating a pause in the birth process, she is to perform an internal examination. If this is clean, they can behave as if she was pure. When the contractions return, they are to behave accordingly.
If the amniotic sac bursts and water flows out, this does not necessarily cause the state of niddah. However, if blood is intermingled with the fluid, she enters the niddah state.
At birth she enters the niddah state. Birth to a stillborn or embryo likewise causes the niddah state.

As explained in Chapter Four, it is forbidden to look at the places of a niddah wife’s body which are normally covered, for example, her legs. Therefore, extra caution must be exercised when she is approaching delivery.
The husband is to refrain from being present in the delivery room during delivery.
The couple should ensure that a “Shir Ham’alos” is placed somewhere in the delivery room, the wife’s and baby’s hospital rooms as well as at home.
As soon as bleeding has ceased after the birth of a son, a woman performs the hefsek tahara, counts the seven white days and immerses in the mikveh.

After the birth of a daughter, the same cycle of purity is observed, with the condition that the mikveh night is at least fourteen days after the birth (the night between the fourteenth and fifteenth day).
The laws of separation, covered in Chapter Four, apply during these times as well.

If, following birth, the wife feels she has not sufficiently recovered or that she has other related medical complications, she should consult a G-d fearing medical consultant and an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws before performing a hefsek tahara.
The niddah state caused through birth is not considered when calculating the next anticipated menstruation.

In families or communities whose custom it is to wait forty or eighty days following the birth of male or female babies (respectively) before immersing, an orthodox Rabbi expert in this field should be consulted if the woman or couple wish to deviate from custom. Note that even these families or communities needn’t observe this period following a miscarriage. In places where this custom is not established it should not be adopted.
There is no custom for a woman to wait forty or eighty days, after the birth of a son or daughter, respectively, before entering a synagogue.
For twenty-four months following birth, whether nursing or not, a woman does not establish a fixed cycle. (As explained in Appendix - Fixed Cycles.)

If the wife gave birth through a Caesarian section and no blood came out of the womb she remains pure. However, if she reached the stage described in the beginning of this chapter (Behavior Preceding Birth) and then a Caesarian section was done, she remains niddah.
A miscarriage results in the niddah state, even if no blood was found.

If a miscarriage occurred up to and including the fortieth day of pregnancy, she performs a hefsek tahara as soon as blood has ceased, counts the seven white days and immerses in the mikveh. The hefsek tahara must be at least from the fifth day after she became impure due to this miscarriage.
If a miscarriage occurred from the forty-first day of pregnancy, the same cycle of purity follows with the condition that immersion in the mikveh is at least fourteen days after the miscarriage.
To assess this period of time, an orthodox Rabbi expert in these laws should be consulted.
